preamble.whatYouWillLearn: You will plan a statistical investigation and decide what data to collect. You will read charts and diagrams and choose the best one for your data. You will find the mode, median, mean and range, and use data to draw sensible conclusions.
preamble.whyItMatters: Data helps people make good decisions instead of guessing. Knowing how to read graphs and averages helps you spot when a chart or a claim is misleading. Statistics questions also appear in every Cambridge maths exam.
realWorld: Checking a rainfall graph before planning an outing in the monsoon season
A hawker stall owner counting which dishes sell best to decide how much to cook
Comparing your test scores across the year using the mean and the range
Reading a pie chart in the news about how people in KL travel to work
Using a Venn diagram to sort classmates who play football, badminton or both

subtopics.title: Planning an investigation
subtopics.summary: Ask statistical questions and decide what data to collect. Data can be categorical (groups), discrete (counted) or continuous (measured).

subtopics.title: Representing data
subtopics.summary: Record and show data with tally charts, frequency tables, bar, pie and waffle charts, line graphs, scatter graphs, dot plots, and Venn and Carroll diagrams, and choose the best one.

subtopics.title: Averages and range
subtopics.summary: Find the mode, median, mean and range of a data set, and decide which average describes the data best.

subtopics.title: Interpreting data and drawing conclusions
subtopics.summary: Spot patterns and trends, compare data sets, see how an unusual value changes the results, and judge whether a conclusion is reliable.

questions.prompt: Which of these is continuous data?
options: The number of pets each pupil has
The heights of pupils in your class
Pupils' favourite fruits
The shoe sizes of pupils in your class
questions.solution: Continuous data is measured and can be any value in a range, such as 142.5 cm. Height is measured, so it is continuous. Number of pets is counted (discrete), fruits are groups (categorical) and shoe sizes come in fixed steps (discrete).

misconceptions.0: Pets are counted in whole numbers (0, 1, 2 ...), so this is discrete data, not continuous.
misconceptions.2: Favourite fruits are names or groups, not numbers. This is categorical data.
misconceptions.3: Shoe sizes only come in fixed steps (such as 4, 4 1/2, 5), so they are discrete. Foot LENGTH would be continuous, but shoe SIZE is not.

questions.prompt: Pupils are asked for their favourite colour. Is this data categorical, discrete or continuous?
questions.solution: The answers are words such as red, blue or green, not numbers. Data sorted into groups or categories is called categorical data.

misconceptions.common: Calling it discrete because you can count how many pupils chose each colour. The data itself is colour names, which are categories.

questions.prompt: True or false: the number of goals scored in a football match is discrete data.
questions.solution: Goals are counted in whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3 ... You cannot score 2.5 goals. Counted data is discrete, so the statement is true.

misconceptions.common: Thinking all number data is continuous. Measured data (length, mass, time) is continuous; counted data is discrete.

questions.prompt: Match each set of data to its type.

left: The mass of each watermelon at a market
The number of people in each car at a toll plaza
The type of transport pupils use to get to school

questions.solution: Mass is measured, so it is continuous. The number of people is counted, so it is discrete. Type of transport (car, bus, walk) is a group name, so it is categorical.

misconceptions.common: Matching mass with discrete because it is a number. Measured quantities such as mass, length and time are continuous.

questions.prompt: Priya wants to answer the question: 'Do pupils who sleep more get higher scores in a spelling test?' Which data should she collect?
options: Only the spelling test scores of the class
The favourite subject of each pupil
The hours of sleep of the 3 pupils with the highest scores only
Each pupil's hours of sleep and that same pupil's spelling score
questions.solution: Her question links two things: sleep and spelling scores. So she needs both pieces of data for each pupil, kept together as pairs, so she can compare them.

misconceptions.0: This shows how well pupils spelled, but not how much they slept, so it cannot show a link with sleep.
misconceptions.1: Favourite subject has nothing to do with this question. Collect data about the two things being compared: sleep and scores.
misconceptions.2: Looking only at the top 3 pupils leaves out everyone else. You need data from all the pupils to see whether more sleep goes with higher scores.

questions.prompt: A statistical question is one you answer by collecting data that varies. Which of these is a statistical question?
options: How many minutes do pupils in Year 6 spend reading each day?
How many minutes are there in one hour?
How old is Arjun today?
What is 15 x 4?
questions.solution: Different Year 6 pupils read for different amounts of time, so you would need to collect data from many pupils to answer it. That makes it a statistical question. The other questions each have one fixed answer.

misconceptions.1: This has one fixed answer (60) that never changes. No data needs to be collected.
misconceptions.2: This has just one answer about one person. A statistical question collects many answers that differ from each other.
misconceptions.3: This is a calculation with one answer (60). No data needs to be collected.

questions.prompt: Arjun is investigating the question: 'How do pupils in our school travel to school?' Select ALL the sensible things he should do.
options: Ask pupils from every year group, not just his own class
Ask only his best friends
Make a tally chart with groups such as walk, car, bus and bicycle
Include an 'other' group for pupils who travel in a different way
Measure each pupil's height
questions.solution: To answer a question about the whole school, he should ask pupils from all year groups. A tally chart with clear groups makes recording quick, and an 'other' group catches answers such as motorbike or train. Asking only friends, or measuring heights, does not help answer the question.

misconceptions.1: Asking only his friends gives a small group who may all travel the same way, so the results would not represent the whole school.
misconceptions.4: Height has nothing to do with how pupils travel to school. Only collect data that helps answer the question.

questions.prompt: True or false: Siti times how long each pupil takes to run 100 m, for example 15.4 seconds. This is discrete data.
questions.solution: Time is measured, not counted, and it can be any value (15.4 s, 15.43 s and so on). That makes it continuous data, so the statement is false.

misconceptions.common: Thinking that a number written with one decimal place is discrete. Measurements such as time, length and mass are continuous, even when they are rounded.

questions.prompt: Omar wants to find out the most popular hawker food among the 600 pupils in his school. Which plan will give him the most reliable answer?
options: Ask the 10 pupils in his football team
Ask 60 pupils who are queuing at the noodle stall
Ask 60 pupils, chosen from every class in the school
Ask his parents which food they think pupils like
questions.solution: A reliable sample is big enough and includes all kinds of pupils. 60 pupils chosen from every class gives a fair mix, so it represents the whole school best.

misconceptions.0: 10 pupils from one team is a very small group, and they may not like the same food as the rest of the school.
misconceptions.1: Pupils queuing for noodles probably like noodles, so the results would unfairly favour noodles. This is called a biased sample.
misconceptions.3: This is a guess by two adults, not data from the pupils themselves.

questions.prompt: Daniel predicts: 'Pupils who spend more time on their phones sleep for fewer hours.' Which is the best way to record his data so he can test his prediction?
options: Two separate lists: all the phone times in order, and all the sleep times in order
A tally chart of pupils' favourite phone apps
A table with one row for each pupil, showing that pupil's phone time and sleep time
A Carroll diagram sorting pupils into boys and girls
questions.solution: To test a link between two things, keep each pupil's two values together as a pair. A table with one row per pupil does this. Later, the pairs can be plotted on a scatter graph.

misconceptions.0: Sorting the two lists separately breaks the pairs. You would no longer know which sleep time belongs to which pupil, so you cannot test the link.
misconceptions.1: Favourite apps do not measure phone time or sleep, so this cannot test his prediction.
misconceptions.3: This sorts pupils into groups but records no phone times or sleep times.

questions.prompt: The tally chart shows the colours of cars that passed the school gate. Each group of five is drawn as four lines with a fifth line across them. How many blue cars passed the school gate?

diagram.title: Cars passing the school gate
diagram.alt: A tally chart with a row of tally marks for each colour of car: red, blue and white.

questions.solution: Look at the blue row. It has 3 complete groups of five and 2 more single lines. Each group = 5, so 3 groups = 3 x 5 = 15. Add the 2 single lines: 15 + 2 = 17 blue cars.

misconceptions.1: You counted each group as 1. Each group stands for 5 cars: 3 x 5 = 15, then add the 2 single lines.
misconceptions.2: You counted the groups (3 x 5 = 15) but forgot the 2 single lines.
misconceptions.3: You counted each group as 4 lines. The line drawn across the four is the fifth, so each group is 5.

questions.skill: reading tally charts and frequency tables

questions.prompt: Which representation is best for showing how the temperature in a classroom changes every hour during one day?
options: A pie chart
A Venn diagram
A tally chart
A line graph
questions.solution: Temperature is continuous data that changes over time. A line graph joins the readings in time order, so you can see the temperature rise and fall during the day.

misconceptions.0: A pie chart shows how one whole is split into parts. It does not show change over time.
misconceptions.1: A Venn diagram sorts items into groups that may overlap. It does not show change over time.
misconceptions.2: A tally chart is for counting how often something happens. Temperature is measured, not counted.

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows how many brothers and sisters (siblings) the pupils in a class have. How many pupils are in the class?

diagram.title: Number of siblings
diagram.alt: A bar chart showing how many brothers and sisters the pupils in a class have.

questions.solution: Read the height of each bar (the number of pupils). 0 siblings: 4 pupils. 1 sibling: 9 pupils. 2 siblings: 6 pupils. 3 siblings: 3 pupils. Add them: 4 + 9 + 6 + 3 = 22 pupils.

misconceptions.common: Adding the numbers along the bottom (0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6) instead of the heights of the bars. The height of each bar tells you how many pupils are in that group.

questions.skill: reading tally charts and frequency tables

questions.prompt: Look at the Venn diagram. Where should the number 12 go?
options: In the 'Multiples of 3' circle only
In the overlap, inside both circles
In the 'Even numbers' circle only
Outside both circles
questions.solution: 12 = 3 x 4, so 12 is a multiple of 3. 12 is also even. It belongs to both groups, so it goes in the overlap where the two circles cross, with 6.

misconceptions.0: 12 is a multiple of 3, but it is also even. A number that fits both labels goes in the overlap.
misconceptions.2: 12 is even, but it is also a multiple of 3 (3 x 4 = 12). It belongs in both circles at once.
misconceptions.3: Numbers outside the circles fit neither label. 12 fits both labels.

questions.prompt: Look at the Carroll diagram. In which box should the number 50 go?
options: Even and not greater than 50
Even and greater than 50
Not even and not greater than 50
Not even and greater than 50
questions.solution: 50 is even, because it ends in 0. 50 is not greater than 50, because it is equal to 50. So it goes in the box for 'Even' and 'Not greater than 50', with 12 and 36.

misconceptions.1: 50 is not greater than 50; it is equal to 50. 'Greater than 50' means 51 or more.
misconceptions.2: 50 ends in 0, so it is even.
misconceptions.3: 50 is even, and it is not greater than 50, so both parts of this box are wrong for 50.

questions.prompt: The pie chart shows how 120 pupils travel to school. The bus sector is marked as a right angle (90°). How many pupils travel by bus?

diagram.title: How pupils travel to school
diagram.alt: Pie chart titled How pupils travel to school, with four sectors: bus, car, walk and bicycle. The bus sector is marked as a right angle.

questions.solution: The bus sector is a right angle, 90°. A full pie chart is 360°. 90° is 90/360 = 1/4 of the circle. 1/4 of 120 pupils = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 pupils.

misconceptions.0: 90 is the angle in degrees, not the number of pupils. Work out what fraction of the whole circle 90° is.
misconceptions.1: You treated the pie chart as if it were out of 100 and found 90% of 120. A full circle is 360°, so 90° is 90/360 = 1/4 of it.
misconceptions.3: You treated 90° as half of the circle. Half a circle is 180°; 90° is a quarter.

questions.skill: reading pie charts and waffle charts

questions.prompt: The waffle chart has 100 small squares and shows the favourite drinks of 200 pupils. The shaded squares show the pupils who chose teh tarik. How many pupils chose teh tarik?
questions.solution: Count the shaded squares: there are 35. 100 squares stand for 200 pupils, so 1 square = 200 ÷ 100 = 2 pupils. 35 squares = 35 x 2 = 70 pupils. (35 squares out of 100 is 35%, and 35% of 200 = 70.)

misconceptions.0: 35 is the number of squares. There are 200 pupils but only 100 squares, so each square stands for 2 pupils.
misconceptions.2: You subtracted 35 from 200. The 35 shaded squares show teh tarik, and each square stands for 2 pupils, so multiply: 35 x 2.
misconceptions.3: You divided 35 by 2 instead of multiplying. Each square stands for 2 pupils, so multiply. You also cannot have half a pupil, which is a clue to check.

questions.skill: reading pie charts and waffle charts

questions.prompt: Pupils in a class each choose their favourite fruit from durian, mango, banana and papaya. Select ALL the representations that would be suitable for showing the results.
options: Bar chart
Pie chart
Line graph
Scatter graph
Frequency table
questions.solution: Favourite fruit is categorical data. A frequency table records how many pupils chose each fruit, a bar chart compares the groups, and a pie chart shows each fruit as a share of the class. Line graphs and scatter graphs are for number data.

misconceptions.2: A line graph shows how something changes over time or along a number scale. Fruits are categories with no order, so joining points with lines makes no sense.
misconceptions.3: A scatter graph needs two sets of number data for each person (such as height and arm span). Favourite fruit is one set of categories.

questions.prompt: The dot plot shows how many books some pupils read in a month. Each dot is one pupil. How many books did these pupils read altogether?
questions.solution: Read the dots: 2 pupils read 1 book, 5 read 2, 3 read 3 and 1 read 4. Multiply each number of books by the number of pupils, then add: 1 x 2 = 2, 2 x 5 = 10, 3 x 3 = 9, 4 x 1 = 4. Total = 2 + 10 + 9 + 4 = 25 books.

misconceptions.common: Adding the dots (2 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 11). That gives the number of PUPILS, not the number of books.

questions.prompt: True or false: a scatter graph is a good way to see whether there is a link between pupils' heights and their arm spans.
questions.solution: A scatter graph plots two measurements for each pupil as one point. If the points go up from left to right, taller pupils tend to have longer arm spans. So the statement is true.

misconceptions.common: Thinking a bar chart or pie chart would be better. Those show one set of data; a scatter graph compares two sets of number data in pairs.

questions.prompt: School A has 200 pupils, and the football sector is 1/4 of its pie chart of favourite sports. School B has 400 pupils, and the football sector is 1/5 of its pie chart. Which statement is correct?
options: More pupils chose football in School A, because its sector is bigger.
The same number of pupils chose football in both schools.
You cannot tell how many pupils chose football in either school.
More pupils chose football in School B, even though its sector is smaller.
questions.solution: School A: 1/4 of 200 = 200 ÷ 4 = 50 pupils. School B: 1/5 of 400 = 400 ÷ 5 = 80 pupils. 80 is more than 50, so more pupils chose football in School B, even though its sector is smaller. Pie charts show fractions, so always check the totals.

misconceptions.0: A bigger sector means a bigger FRACTION, not more pupils. School A: 1/4 of 200 = 50. School B: 1/5 of 400 = 80.
misconceptions.1: Work out each one: 1/4 of 200 = 50 and 1/5 of 400 = 80. They are not the same.
misconceptions.2: You can, because you know the total number of pupils in each school. Multiply the fraction by the total.

questions.skill: reading pie charts and waffle charts

questions.prompt: The table shows the favourite sports of 36 pupils and the angle each sport will have on a pie chart. What angle should the swimming sector be? Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: A full circle is 360°, shared among 36 pupils. Each pupil gets 360 ÷ 36 = 10°. Swimming has 5 pupils: 5 x 10° = 50°. Check: 120° + 100° + 50° + 90° = 360°.

misconceptions.common: Treating the pie chart as if it were out of 100, or writing 5° for 5 pupils. A pie chart is a full circle of 360°, so first find the angle for one pupil.

questions.prompt: In a class of 30 pupils, 18 have a cat, 12 have a dog and 5 have both a cat and a dog. The Venn diagram shows the 5 pupils who have both. How many pupils have neither a cat nor a dog?
questions.solution: The 5 in the overlap have both pets. Cat only = 18 - 5 = 13. Dog only = 12 - 5 = 7. Pupils with a cat, a dog or both = 13 + 5 + 7 = 25. Neither (outside both circles) = 30 - 25 = 5.

misconceptions.common: Adding 18 + 12 = 30 and answering 0. The 5 pupils with both pets are counted twice that way, once in each circle.

questions.prompt: Find the mode of these numbers: 5, 9, 3, 9, 11, 4, 9, 6
questions.solution: The mode is the value that appears most often. 9 appears three times, more than any other number. So the mode is 9.

misconceptions.0: 3 is how many times 9 appears. The mode is the value itself, not how often it appears.
misconceptions.1: 7.5 is the median (the middle of the ordered list). The mode is the value that appears most often.
misconceptions.2: 8 is the range (11 - 3). The mode is the value that appears most often.

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows the midday temperature in Penang on five days. Find the range. Give your answer in °C.
questions.solution: Read the bars: 31, 28, 33, 30 and 26 °C. The highest is 33 °C (Wednesday) and the lowest is 26 °C (Friday). Range = highest value - lowest value = 33 - 26 = 7 °C.

misconceptions.common: Subtracting the first and last bars (Monday 31 - Friday 26 = 5). Find the tallest and the shortest bars first.

questions.prompt: Find the mean of these numbers: 6, 9, 4, 11, 10
questions.solution: Add the numbers: 6 + 9 + 4 + 11 + 10 = 40. There are 5 numbers. Mean = 40 ÷ 5 = 8.

misconceptions.0: 40 is the total. To find the mean, divide the total by how many numbers there are: 40 ÷ 5.
misconceptions.2: 9 is the median (the middle number when the list is in order: 4, 6, 9, 10, 11).
misconceptions.3: 7 is the range (11 - 4). The mean is the total shared out equally.

questions.prompt: Find the median of these numbers: 12, 5, 15, 9, 7
questions.solution: First put the numbers in order: 5, 7, 9, 12, 15. The median is the middle value, which is 9.

misconceptions.common: Taking the middle number of the list without putting the list in order first, which gives 15.

questions.prompt: Find the median of these numbers: 14, 8, 11, 20, 5, 16
questions.solution: In order: 5, 8, 11, 14, 16, 20. There are 6 values, so there are two middle values: 11 and 14. The median is halfway between them: (11 + 14) ÷ 2 = 25 ÷ 2 = 12.5.

misconceptions.0: 11 is one of the two middle values. With an even number of values, the median is halfway between the two middle values.
misconceptions.1: You added the two middle values (11 + 14 = 25) but forgot to halve.
misconceptions.3: 15 is the range (20 - 5), not the median.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the modes of this data set: 3, 5, 5, 6, 8, 8, 9
questions.solution: 5 appears twice and 8 appears twice. Every other value appears once. So there are two modes, 5 and 8. Data with two modes is called bimodal.

misconceptions.common: Choosing only one mode. When two values are tied for appearing most often, the data is bimodal and both values are modes.
misconceptions.2: 6 is the median (the middle value), not a mode. It appears only once.

questions.prompt: The mean of four numbers is 15. Three of the numbers are 12, 18 and 10. What is the fourth number?
questions.solution: Total of the four numbers = mean x 4 = 15 x 4 = 60. The three known numbers add up to 12 + 18 + 10 = 40. Fourth number = 60 - 40 = 20.

misconceptions.common: Answering 15 because the mean is 15. The mean is the total shared out equally, so work with the total: 15 x 4 = 60.

questions.skill: using the mean to find a missing value

questions.prompt: The weekly pocket money of 6 friends is RM 10, RM 12, RM 11, RM 10, RM 13 and RM 80. Which average best describes how much a typical friend gets?
options: The median, because the RM 80 pulls the mean up
The mean, because it uses every value
The range, because it shows the biggest and smallest amounts
The mode, because the mode is always the best average
questions.solution: Put the amounts in order: 10, 10, 11, 12, 13, 80. The median is (11 + 12) ÷ 2 = RM 11.50, which is close to what most friends get. The mean is 136 ÷ 6, about RM 22.67, pulled up by the unusual RM 80. So the median is the best average here.

misconceptions.1: The mean is RM 136 ÷ 6, about RM 22.67, which is more than five of the six friends get. One very large value (RM 80) pulls the mean up, so it is not typical.
misconceptions.2: The range (RM 80 - RM 10 = RM 70) measures how spread out the data is. It is not an average.
misconceptions.3: No average is always the best. Here the mode (RM 10) is the lowest amount, so it does not show the middle of the data as well as the median.

questions.prompt: True or false: for the numbers 2, 4, 6 and 100, the mean is less than the median.
questions.solution: Mean = (2 + 4 + 6 + 100) ÷ 4 = 112 ÷ 4 = 28. Median = (4 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5. The mean (28) is MORE than the median (5), so the statement is false. The large value 100 pulls the mean up.

misconceptions.common: Forgetting that one very large value pulls the mean up a lot but hardly changes the median.

questions.prompt: The mean mass of 5 durians is 1.8 kg. A sixth durian is added, and the mean mass of all 6 durians becomes 2 kg. What is the mass of the sixth durian? Give your answer in kg.
questions.solution: Total mass of 5 durians = 5 x 1.8 = 9 kg. Total mass of 6 durians = 6 x 2 = 12 kg. Sixth durian = 12 - 9 = 3 kg.

misconceptions.common: Answering 0.2 kg (2 - 1.8), which is only the change in the mean. Work with the totals instead: the new durian has to raise the mean of all six durians.

questions.skill: using the mean to find a missing value

questions.prompt: A set of five whole numbers has a mode of 4, a median of 6 and a mean of 7. Which set could it be?
questions.solution: Check all three averages for 4, 4, 6, 9, 12. 4 appears twice, so the mode is 4. The middle value is 6, so the median is 6. The total is 4 + 4 + 6 + 9 + 12 = 35, and 35 ÷ 5 = 7, so the mean is 7. All three match.

misconceptions.0: The mode (4) and median (6) are right, but the total is 32 and 32 ÷ 5 = 6.4, so the mean is not 7.
misconceptions.2: 6 appears twice, so the mode is 6, not 4. (The median is 6 and the mean is 35 ÷ 5 = 7, so only the mode is wrong.)
misconceptions.3: The mode (4) and mean (35 ÷ 5 = 7) are right, but the middle value is 7, so the median is 7, not 6.

questions.prompt: Priya's mean score in 4 spelling tests is 16. Each test is marked out of 25. What score does she need in the 5th test to make her mean score for all 5 tests exactly 17?
questions.solution: Total so far = 4 x 16 = 64. For a mean of 17 over 5 tests, the total must be 5 x 17 = 85. Score needed = 85 - 64 = 21. (21 is less than 25, so it is possible.)

misconceptions.common: Answering 17 or 18, thinking she only needs to score a little above her mean. The extra marks are shared over all 5 tests, so work with the totals.

questions.skill: using the mean to find a missing value

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows the number of ice creams sold at a stall each day. How many more ice creams were sold on the best day than on the worst day?

diagram.title: Ice creams sold
diagram.alt: A bar chart of the number of ice creams sold at a stall on each day from Monday to Friday.

questions.solution: The tallest bar is Friday: 35 ice creams. The shortest bar is Tuesday: 18 ice creams. 35 - 18 = 17 more ice creams.

misconceptions.common: Using Monday as the worst day because it comes first. Look at all the bars to find the shortest, which is Tuesday (18).

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows the rainfall in a Malaysian town from October to December. True or false: the rainfall increased every month from October to December.
questions.solution: Read the bars: October 250 mm, November 290 mm, December 220 mm. From October to November the rainfall increased. But from November to December it decreased (the December bar is shorter). So it did not increase every month, and the statement is false.

misconceptions.common: Checking only the first two months. Check every step of a pattern before deciding.

questions.prompt: The scatter graph shows the temperature on different days (across the bottom) and the number of cold drinks a school canteen sold on those days (up the side). Which statement best describes the graph?
options: The hotter the day, the more cold drinks were sold.
The hotter the day, the fewer cold drinks were sold.
There is no link between temperature and cold drink sales.
Selling cold drinks makes the weather hotter.
questions.solution: Points going up from left to right show that when one value goes up, the other tends to go up too. So hotter days go with more cold drinks sold.

misconceptions.1: Points going up from left to right mean both values get bigger together. Fewer drinks on hotter days would show points going DOWN from left to right.
misconceptions.2: No link would look like points scattered everywhere with no pattern. Here the points go up together.
misconceptions.3: The graph shows that the two things go together, but drinks cannot change the weather. A link between two things does not mean one causes the other.

questions.prompt: The line graph shows the height of a plant each week. Between which two weeks did the plant grow the most?
options: Between Week 3 and Week 4
Between Week 0 and Week 1
Between Week 2 and Week 3
Between Week 1 and Week 2
questions.solution: Read the points: 2, 5, 9, 14 and 16 cm. Find each increase. Week 0 to 1: 3 cm. Week 1 to 2: 4 cm. Week 2 to 3: 5 cm. Week 3 to 4: 2 cm. The biggest increase is 5 cm, between Week 2 and Week 3. This is the steepest part of the line.

misconceptions.0: Week 4 has the greatest height, but the plant only grew 16 - 14 = 2 cm that week. Look at the increase, not the height.
misconceptions.1: The plant grew 5 - 2 = 3 cm here, which is less than 14 - 9 = 5 cm.
misconceptions.3: The plant grew 9 - 5 = 4 cm here, which is less than 14 - 9 = 5 cm.

questions.prompt: Two classes took the same quiz, marked out of 20. Class A: mean 14, range 3. Class B: mean 14, range 12. Which statement is correct?
options: Class B did better, because its range is bigger.
Class A did better on average, because its range is smaller.
Class B's scores were more consistent, because its range is bigger.
On average both classes did equally well, but Class A's scores were more consistent.
questions.solution: The means are the same (14), so on average the classes did equally well. Class A's range (3) is much smaller than Class B's (12), so Class A's scores were closer together, which means more consistent.

misconceptions.0: The range shows how spread out the scores are, not how high they are. Both classes have the same mean, 14.
misconceptions.1: A smaller range means the scores were closer together, not higher. The means are the same, so on average the classes did equally well.
misconceptions.2: A bigger range means the scores were MORE spread out, so Class B was less consistent.

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows the number of visitors to a park each year. Select ALL the statements that are true.
options: The number of visitors never went down from one year to the next.
The biggest increase was from 2024 to 2025.
The number of visitors doubled from 2022 to 2025.
The mean number of visitors per year was 1525.
The number of visitors went up every year.
questions.solution: Read the bars: 1200, 1500, 1500 and 1900. Changes: 2022 to 2023: up 300. 2023 to 2024: no change. 2024 to 2025: up 400. So the number never went down, and the biggest increase (400) was from 2024 to 2025. It did not go up every year, because 2023 and 2024 were the same. Double 1200 is 2400, not 1900. Mean = (1200 + 1500 + 1500 + 1900) ÷ 4 = 6100 ÷ 4 = 1525. The true statements are the first, second and fourth.

misconceptions.2: Double 1200 is 2400. The visitors grew to 1900, which is less than double.
misconceptions.4: From 2023 to 2024 the number stayed the same (1500), so it did not go up every year. 'Never went down' and 'went up every year' mean different things.

questions.prompt: Put these sets of data in order from most consistent (smallest range) to least consistent (largest range).
questions.solution: Range = highest - lowest. A: 12 - 4 = 8. B: 25 - 20 = 5. C: 15 - 1 = 14. D: 45 - 30 = 15. From smallest to largest range: B (5), A (8), C (14), D (15).

misconceptions.common: Ordering by the size of the numbers instead of by the range. Set B has bigger numbers than Set A, but its values are closer together.

questions.prompt: Aisha asked 5 pupils in her class to name their favourite subject, and 3 of them said art. She concludes: 'Art is the favourite subject of most pupils in our school.' What is the best reason why her conclusion may not be reliable?
options: She asked only 5 pupils from one class, so the sample is too small to represent the whole school.
3 out of 5 is less than half, so art is not the most popular.
She should have drawn a pie chart instead of writing the numbers down.
Art cannot be a favourite subject because it is not tested in exams.
questions.solution: A conclusion about a whole school needs data from many pupils in different classes. 5 pupils from one class is too few and may not be typical, so her conclusion may not be reliable. She could ask more pupils from every class to check her idea.

misconceptions.1: 3 out of 5 is 60%, which is more than half. The problem is not the fraction but how few pupils were asked.
misconceptions.2: Changing the chart does not change the data. A pie chart of 5 answers is still based on only 5 pupils.
misconceptions.3: Any subject can be someone's favourite. This is an opinion, not a problem with the data.

questions.prompt: Five pupils took 8, 10, 9, 11 and 12 minutes to walk to school. A sixth pupil took 40 minutes. By how many minutes does the mean time go up when the sixth pupil is included?
questions.solution: Mean of the first five = (8 + 10 + 9 + 11 + 12) ÷ 5 = 50 ÷ 5 = 10 minutes. Mean of all six = (50 + 40) ÷ 6 = 90 ÷ 6 = 15 minutes. The mean goes up by 15 - 10 = 5 minutes. One unusual value (an outlier) can change the mean a lot.

misconceptions.common: Answering 15, the new mean, instead of how much the mean went up. Another slip is dividing 90 by 5 instead of 6: there are now 6 pupils.

questions.prompt: The mean of 6 test scores is 70. One score of 40 turns out to be a recording mistake, so it is removed. What is the mean of the 5 scores that are left?
questions.solution: Total of the 6 scores = 6 x 70 = 420. Remove the 40: 420 - 40 = 380. Mean of the 5 scores = 380 ÷ 5 = 76.

misconceptions.common: Dividing by 6 again after removing a score. There are only 5 scores left, so divide by 5.

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows the number of books borrowed from the school library each day. How many books were borrowed on Thursday?

diagram.title: Books borrowed from the library
diagram.alt: Bar chart titled Books borrowed from the library, with one bar for each day from Monday to Friday. The scale goes from 0 to 30 in steps of 5, with small gridlines every 1.

questions.solution: Find the bar for Thu. Go across from the top of the bar to the scale. The top is 2 small gridlines above 15. Each small gridline is 1 book, so 15 + 2 = 17 books.

misconceptions.common: Reading the labelled line just below the top of the bar (15) and forgetting the small gridlines. There are 5 small spaces between 15 and 20, so each one is worth 1 book.

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows the favourite fruits of the boys and girls in Year 6. For which fruit is the difference between the number of boys and the number of girls the greatest?
options: Durian
Mango
Banana
Papaya
questions.solution: Read each pair of bars and subtract the smaller from the larger. Durian: 8 - 6 = 2. Mango: 15 - 12 = 3. Banana: 9 - 5 = 4. Papaya: 7 - 4 = 3. The greatest difference is 4, for banana.

misconceptions.0: Durian has 8 boys and 6 girls, a difference of only 2. Banana has a difference of 9 - 5 = 4.
misconceptions.1: Mango has the tallest bars, so it is the most popular fruit, but the gap is only 15 - 12 = 3. The question asks about the gap between the two bars.
misconceptions.3: Papaya has 7 boys and 4 girls, a difference of 3. Banana's gap is bigger: 9 - 5 = 4.

questions.prompt: The line graph shows the temperature in a school garden during one day. What was the temperature at 11 am? Give your answer in °C.

diagram.title: Temperature in the school garden
diagram.alt: Line graph titled Temperature in the school garden, with a point at 7 am, 9 am, 11 am, 1 pm, 3 pm and 5 pm. The scale goes from 24 to 34 °C in steps of 2, with small gridlines every 1 °C.

questions.solution: Find 11 am on the bottom axis. Go up to the point on the line, then across to the scale. The point is on the small gridline halfway between 30 and 32. The temperature was 31 °C.

misconceptions.common: Reading the labelled line below the point (30) or the point for a different time. The scale goes up in 2s, so the small gridline halfway between 30 and 32 is 31.

questions.prompt: The line graph shows the number of durians a stall sold each week. Between which two weeks did the sales fall the most?
options: Week 2 to Week 3
Week 3 to Week 4
Week 4 to Week 5
Week 5 to Week 6
questions.solution: Read the points: 120, 150, 140, 190, 170, 110. Find each change. Week 1 to 2: up 30. Week 2 to 3: down 10. Week 3 to 4: up 50. Week 4 to 5: down 20. Week 5 to 6: down 60. The biggest fall is 60, from Week 5 to Week 6. It is the steepest downward part of the line.

misconceptions.0: Sales did fall from Week 2 to Week 3, but only by 150 - 140 = 10.
misconceptions.1: From Week 3 to Week 4 the line goes UP by 50. That is the biggest rise, not a fall.
misconceptions.2: Sales fell by 190 - 170 = 20 here. The fall from Week 5 to Week 6 is bigger: 170 - 110 = 60.

questions.prompt: The pie chart shows the favourite hawker food of 72 pupils. The angle of each sector is shown. How many pupils chose satay?

diagram.title: Favourite hawker food
diagram.alt: Pie chart titled Favourite hawker food. Nasi lemak 120°, roti canai 90°, satay 60°, mee goreng 90°.

questions.solution: The satay sector is 60°. A full circle is 360°, so satay is 60/360 = 1/6 of the circle. 1/6 of 72 = 72 ÷ 6 = 12 pupils. (Or: each pupil gets 360 ÷ 72 = 5°, and 60 ÷ 5 = 12.)

misconceptions.common: Answering 60 (the angle), or finding 60% of 72. The angle is in degrees out of 360, not a number of pupils or a percentage. Find what fraction of 360° the sector is, then take that fraction of 72.

questions.skill: reading pie charts and waffle charts

questions.prompt: Mei Lin made this tally chart of her classmates' favourite fruits. What number should go in the box for mango in the Frequency column?

diagram.title: Favourite fruits
diagram.alt: Tally chart with columns Fruit, Tally and Frequency. Durian 8, banana 6 and rambutan 11 are filled in. Mango has tally marks and a box for its frequency.

questions.solution: Count the mango tally marks in fives. There are 2 complete groups of five (2 x 5 = 10) and 3 single lines. 10 + 3 = 13.

misconceptions.common: Counting each group as 4 lines, or as 1. A group is four lines with a fifth line across them, so it stands for 5.

questions.skill: reading tally charts and frequency tables

questions.prompt: Look at the Venn diagram. Which number could go in the box?
questions.solution: The box is outside both circles, so the number must be neither a multiple of 4 nor a factor of 36. 6 and 2 are factors of 36. 20 is a multiple of 4. 11 is not a multiple of 4, and 36 ÷ 11 is not a whole number, so 11 is not a factor of 36. The answer is 11.

misconceptions.0: 6 is a factor of 36 (6 x 6 = 36), so it belongs in the 'Factors of 36' circle, not outside.
misconceptions.1: 20 = 4 x 5, so it is a multiple of 4. It belongs in the 'Multiples of 4' circle.
misconceptions.3: 2 is a factor of 36 (2 x 18 = 36), so it belongs in the 'Factors of 36' circle.

questions.prompt: Kumar sorted some numbers in the Carroll diagram. He put one number in the wrong box. Which number is in the wrong box?
questions.solution: Check each number against its row AND its column. 15 and 35 are odd multiples of 5. 7 and 21 are odd and not multiples of 5. 20 is an even multiple of 5. 8 and 14 are even and not multiples of 5. 45 is a multiple of 5, but it ends in 5, so it is odd. It should be in the 'Odd' row, not the 'Not odd' row.

misconceptions.common: Checking only the column heading. Each number must fit BOTH its row and its column: 45 is a multiple of 5, but it is odd, so it is in the wrong row.

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows how many eggs Ahmad's hens laid each day from Monday to Friday. On Saturday they laid some more eggs. The mean number of eggs per day for the six days was 12. How many eggs did the hens lay on Saturday?
questions.solution: Read the bars: 12, 9, 14, 10 and 11. Total for Monday to Friday = 12 + 9 + 14 + 10 + 11 = 56. For a mean of 12 over 6 days, the total must be 6 x 12 = 72. Saturday = 72 - 56 = 16 eggs.

misconceptions.common: Answering 12 (the mean), or finding the mean of the five bars. Use totals: the six days must add up to 6 x 12 = 72, so Saturday is 72 minus the total of the five bars.

questions.skill: using the mean to find a missing value

questions.prompt: The table shows the number of goals the school football team scored in each of its 15 matches. What is the median number of goals per match?
questions.solution: There are 3 + 5 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 matches. The median is the middle match when they are listed in order of goals: the 8th. Matches 1 to 3 scored 0 goals. Matches 4 to 8 scored 1 goal. So the 8th match scored 1 goal, and the median is 1.

misconceptions.common: Finding the middle of the 'Number of matches' column (3, 5, 4, 2, 1 in order gives 3), or taking the middle row (2 goals). The median is the middle MATCH when all 15 are listed in order of goals.

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows the shoe sizes of the pupils in a class. What is the mode of the shoe sizes?
questions.solution: The mode is the value that appears most often. The tallest bar is for size 35 (9 pupils). So the mode is shoe size 35.

misconceptions.0: 9 is the number of pupils with the most common size (the height of the tallest bar). The mode is the shoe size itself: 35.
misconceptions.2: 37 is the largest shoe size, not the most common. Look for the tallest bar.
misconceptions.3: Size 34 has 7 pupils, but size 35 has more (9).

questions.prompt: Wei Ming measured the temperature of a cup of hot tea every 5 minutes for 25 minutes. He drew his results in three ways. Which chart is the best way to show how the temperature changed over time?
options: Chart A
Chart B
Chart C
questions.solution: The temperature is a measurement that changes over time, and a line graph is the chart for showing change over time: the line shows the tea cooling quickly at first, then more slowly, and you can read times in between. Chart C is the line graph. Chart A (a bar chart) shows each reading as a separate bar, and Chart B (a pie chart) shows parts of a whole, which makes no sense for temperatures.

misconceptions.0: A bar chart can show the readings, but a line graph is better for a measurement that changes over time, like temperature. The line shows the change between readings.
misconceptions.1: A pie chart shows how a whole is split into parts. Temperatures at different times do not add up to a whole, so a pie chart makes no sense here.

questions.prompt: Siti asked 40 pupils to choose their favourite sport. She drew her results in three ways. Which chart shows most clearly what fraction of the 40 pupils chose each sport?
options: Chart A
Chart B
Chart C
questions.solution: A pie chart shows how a whole is split into parts, so you can see what fraction of all 40 pupils chose each sport. Chart B is the pie chart: for example, badminton (15 out of 40) is a bit more than a third of the circle. The bar chart (Chart C) is good for comparing the numbers, but it does not show the whole class. The line graph (Chart A) should not be used, because the sports are separate groups, not changes over time.

misconceptions.0: A line graph joins points to show change over time. The sports are separate groups, so a line between them means nothing.
misconceptions.2: A bar chart is good for comparing how many pupils chose each sport, but it does not show each sport as a part of the whole class. A pie chart does.

questions.prompt: School P has 200 pupils and 50 of them chose football as their favourite sport, so football is 1/4 of School P's pie chart. School Q has 400 pupils and 80 of them chose football. Which pie chart could be School Q's?
options: Pie chart A
Pie chart B
Pie chart C
Pie chart D
questions.solution: Football in School Q = 80 out of 400 = 80/400. Divide the top and bottom by 80: 80/400 = 1/5. So School Q's football sector is 1/5 of the circle: Pie chart D. It is smaller than School P's 1/4, even though more pupils chose football (80, not 50), because School Q has twice as many pupils.

misconceptions.0: 1/4 is School P's fraction. School Q has a different total, so work out its own fraction: 80/400 = 1/5.
misconceptions.1: 2/5 is 80 out of 200, but School Q has 400 pupils, not 200. Use School Q's own total: 80/400 = 1/5.
misconceptions.2: More pupils chose football in School Q, but that does not make its sector bigger. A pie chart shows the fraction of the school: 80/400 = 1/5, which is much less than half.

questions.prompt: The pie chart shows the favourite sports of the 60 pupils in Year 5. In Year 6 there are 30 pupils, and badminton is half of Year 6's pie chart. True or false: more pupils chose badminton in Year 6 than in Year 5.
questions.solution: Year 5: badminton is 1/3 of the pie chart. 1/3 of 60 = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 pupils. Year 6: badminton is 1/2 of 30 = 15 pupils. 15 is fewer than 20, so the statement is false. Year 6's badminton sector is bigger, but Year 6 has only half as many pupils.

misconceptions.common: Comparing the sizes of the sectors. A bigger sector means a bigger FRACTION of that group, not more pupils. Work out the number of pupils from each total first.

questions.prompt: The table shows four tallies, A to D. Match each tally to its frequency.

diagram.title: Four tallies
diagram.alt: A table with four rows, A, B, C and D, each with a tally.

questions.solution: Count in fives, then add the single lines. A: 1 group of five and 2 lines = 7. B: 2 groups and 2 lines = 12. C: 1 group and 4 lines = 9. D: 3 groups and no single lines = 15.

misconceptions.common: Counting a group as 4 lines (then D would look like 12 instead of 15). The fifth line across each group counts too, so every group is 5.

questions.skill: reading tally charts and frequency tables

questions.prompt: The line graph shows the monthly rainfall in two Malaysian towns, Town A and Town B, from September to January. Select ALL the statements that are true.
options: Town B had more rain than Town A in every month.
Both towns had the most rain in November.
The difference between the two towns was greatest in December.
Town A's rainfall went up every month.
In January, Town B had 100 mm more rain than Town A.
Town A had more than twice as much rain in November as in January.
questions.solution: Read the points (each small gridline is 50 mm). Town A: 150, 250, 300, 200, 150 mm. Town B: 200, 350, 650, 500, 250 mm. Town B is higher every month, and both towns are highest in November, so the first two statements are true. The differences are 50, 100, 350, 300 and 100 mm, so the greatest difference is in November, not December. Town A goes down after November. In January, 250 - 150 = 100 mm: true. In November Town A had 300 mm, which is exactly twice January's 150 mm, not more than twice. The true statements are the first, second and fifth.

misconceptions.2: In December the gap is 500 - 200 = 300 mm, but in November it is 650 - 300 = 350 mm.
misconceptions.3: Town A's line goes down after November (300 to 200 to 150 mm).
misconceptions.5: 300 is exactly 2 x 150, so it is twice as much, not MORE than twice.
misconceptions.common: Read each point carefully against the gridlines: the labelled lines go up in 100s and each small gridline is 50 mm.

questions.prompt: Lina predicts: 'More pupils in my class walk to school than come by car.' Which data should she collect to test her prediction?
options: The time each pupil in her class wakes up
How each pupil in her class travels to school
The number of cars in the school car park
How far the school is from the nearest bus stop
questions.solution: Her prediction compares two ways of travelling: walking and coming by car. So she needs to know how each pupil in her class travels to school. Then she can count the walkers and the car pupils and compare the two numbers. The answer is: how each pupil in her class travels to school.

misconceptions.0: Waking-up time does not tell her how pupils travel. Collect data about the thing in the prediction: walking or coming by car.
misconceptions.2: Many cars in the car park belong to teachers and visitors, and one car can bring several pupils. Ask each pupil how they travel instead.
misconceptions.3: This is one fact about the school, not data about the pupils. Her prediction is about how each pupil travels.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of data to the best way to collect it.

left: The favourite hawker food of each pupil
The number of buses that pass the school gate in 30 minutes
The hand span of each pupil
The time each pupil takes to run 50 m

questions.solution: A favourite food is an opinion, so ask each pupil. Buses passing the gate are counted as they happen, so watch and make a tally. A hand span is a length, so measure it with a ruler. A running time is measured with a stopwatch. Hand span and running time are continuous data: they are measured, not counted.

misconceptions.common: Mixing up asking, counting and measuring. Ask people for their opinions, count things that happen with a tally, measure lengths with a ruler and times with a stopwatch.

questions.prompt: Siti predicts: 'Year 6 pupils sleep fewer hours on school nights than Year 4 pupils.' Which plan is the fairest way to test her prediction?
options: Ask 30 Year 6 pupils how long they slept last night
Ask 30 Year 6 pupils and 3 Year 4 pupils how long they slept last night
Ask 30 Year 6 pupils the morning after a school camp, and 30 Year 4 pupils after a normal school night
Ask 30 Year 6 pupils and 30 Year 4 pupils, chosen from several classes in each year, how long they slept on the same school night
questions.solution: To compare two groups fairly: ask both groups, ask a similar number in each, choose pupils from different classes, and ask about the same kind of night. Only the last plan does all of these. Trap: a plan can ask enough pupils and still be unfair if the groups are measured in different conditions.

misconceptions.0: Her prediction compares two year groups. With only Year 6 data there is nothing to compare with.
misconceptions.1: 3 Year 4 pupils is far too few: one unusual sleeper could change the result. Ask a similar number of pupils in each year group.
misconceptions.2: A camp night is not a normal school night, so the two groups are not asked about the same kind of night. In a fair test only the year group changes.

questions.prompt: Daniel is planning an investigation: 'Do taller pupils jump further in the standing long jump?' Select ALL the statements that are true.
options: He should measure the jumps to the nearest whole metre.
Height is continuous data.
He must record each pupil's height and jump distance together, as a pair.
Jump distance is discrete data, because you can count the centimetres.
A scatter graph would help him see whether there is a link.
questions.solution: Height and jump distance are both measured, so both are continuous data. To test a link, he must keep each pupil's two measurements together as a pair, then plot the pairs on a scatter graph. Measuring to the nearest whole metre is far too rough: almost every jump would be recorded as 1 m or 2 m. The true statements are: height is continuous; record the pairs; a scatter graph would help.

misconceptions.0: Most standing jumps are between 1 m and 2 m, so to the nearest metre almost every jump would be 1 m or 2 m and the differences would disappear. Measure to the nearest centimetre.
misconceptions.3: Jump distance is measured, not counted, and it can be any value, such as 1.37 m. That makes it continuous data. The centimetre marks are just how a tape measure shows a measurement.
misconceptions.common: Check each statement on its own. Measured data (height, distance, time) is continuous; to test a link, keep each pupil's two values together.

questions.prompt: Priya predicted: 'More than half of the pupils in Year 6 will choose nasi lemak as their favourite breakfast.' She asked all 36 pupils in Year 6. The bar chart shows her results. Was her prediction correct? Tick one answer with its reason.

diagram.title: Favourite breakfast of Year 6 pupils
diagram.alt: A bar chart of the favourite breakfasts of the 36 Year 6 pupils: nasi lemak, roti canai, bread and cereal.

options: Yes, because more pupils chose nasi lemak than any other breakfast.
Yes, because 14 is more than half of 36.
No, because half of 36 is 18, and only 14 pupils chose nasi lemak.
No, because she should have asked more than 36 pupils.
questions.solution: Read the nasi lemak bar: 14 pupils. Half of 36 = 36 ÷ 2 = 18. 14 is less than 18, so fewer than half of the pupils chose nasi lemak. Nasi lemak is the most popular breakfast, but the prediction said 'more than half', so the prediction was not correct. Trap: 'the most popular' is not the same as 'more than half'.

misconceptions.0: Nasi lemak is the most popular, but that is not what she predicted. 'More than half' means more than 18 of the 36 pupils, and only 14 chose it.
misconceptions.1: Half of 36 is 36 ÷ 2 = 18. 14 is less than 18, so 14 is less than half.
misconceptions.3: She asked all 36 pupils in Year 6, so her data covers the whole year group. The reason is in the result itself: 14 is less than half of 36.

questions.prompt: Omar's main question is: 'How do pupils in our school spend their free time at weekends?' He writes some smaller questions to help him answer it. A statistical question is answered by collecting data that varies. Select ALL the smaller questions that are statistical AND help to answer his main question.
options: What time does the school gate open on Monday?
How many hours do pupils spend on screens at weekends?
Which weekend activity do the most pupils take part in?
How many hours did Omar spend reading last Saturday?
How many days are there in a weekend?
Do older pupils spend more time on sport at weekends than younger pupils?
questions.solution: Check each question twice: does it need data from many pupils that varies, and is it about free time at weekends? Screen time at weekends, the most popular weekend activity, and comparing older and younger pupils all pass both checks. The gate time and the number of days in a weekend have one fixed answer, and Omar's own reading time is about one person only.

misconceptions.0: This has one fixed answer, and it is about school, not free time at weekends.
misconceptions.3: This is about one person only, so the answer does not vary. A statistical question collects data from many pupils.
misconceptions.4: This has one fixed answer (2 days). No data needs to be collected.
misconceptions.common: A statistical question needs data from many people, and the answers vary. It must also help with the main question.

questions.prompt: Aisha predicts: 'Most pupils in my class spend between 1 and 2 hours on homework each day.' She is writing a questionnaire to test this. Which set of answer boxes should she use?
options: Less than 1 hour; 1 hour to less than 2 hours; 2 hours or more
0 to 1 hour; 1 to 2 hours; 2 to 3 hours
1 to 2 hours; 3 to 4 hours; 5 to 6 hours
A little; Some; A lot
questions.solution: Homework time is continuous data, so the answer boxes must be number groups with no overlaps and no gaps, so every pupil ticks exactly one box. 'Less than 1 hour', '1 hour to less than 2 hours' and '2 hours or more' do this, and the middle box matches the group in her prediction. A pupil who does exactly 2 hours ticks '2 hours or more'. Trap: '0 to 1' and '1 to 2' both contain 1 hour.

misconceptions.1: These groups overlap: a pupil who does exactly 1 hour or exactly 2 hours could tick two boxes. A pupil who does more than 3 hours has no box at all.
misconceptions.2: There are gaps: a pupil who does 30 minutes or 2 1/2 hours has no box to tick. Every possible answer needs exactly one box.
misconceptions.3: 'A little' means different things to different people, so she cannot tell who does between 1 and 2 hours. Use groups with numbers.

questions.prompt: The pie chart shows the favourite drinks of some pupils. What fraction of the pupils chose Milo?

diagram.title: Favourite drinks
diagram.alt: Pie chart titled Favourite drinks with three sectors: Milo, teh tarik and orange juice. The teh tarik and orange juice sectors are each marked as a right angle.

questions.solution: The teh tarik and orange juice sectors are right angles, so each is 1/4 of the circle. Together they make 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. That leaves 1 - 1/2 = 1/2 for Milo, and its edges make a straight line through the centre. So 1/2 of the pupils chose Milo.

misconceptions.0: There are 3 sectors, but they are not the same size. The Milo sector is half of the circle: its two edges make one straight line through the centre.
misconceptions.1: 1/4 is the size of each smaller sector (each is marked as a right angle). The Milo sector is two right angles, so it is twice as big.
misconceptions.3: 3/4 would be three right angles. The Milo sector is two right angles, which is 2/4 = 1/2.

questions.skill: reading pie charts and waffle charts

questions.prompt: The pie chart shows what some pupils like to do at break time. What percentage of the pupils like reading best?

diagram.title: Favourite break-time activity
diagram.alt: Pie chart titled Favourite break-time activity with four sectors: games 50%, eating 25% (marked as a right angle), reading (percentage not shown) and chatting 10%.

questions.solution: The whole pie chart is 100%. Add the percentages you know: 50% + 25% + 10% = 85%. Reading is the rest: 100% - 85% = 15%.

misconceptions.common: Forgetting that the whole pie chart is 100%. Add the percentages you know (50 + 25 + 10 = 85), then take that away from 100.

questions.skill: reading pie charts and waffle charts

questions.prompt: The pie chart shows the favourite fruits of some pupils, but the key is missing. Durian is 50%, mango is 25%, banana is 15% and papaya is 10%. Match each fruit to its sector on the pie chart.

diagram.title: Favourite fruits
diagram.alt: Pie chart titled Favourite fruits with four sectors labelled A, B, C and D, clockwise from the top. One sector is marked as a right angle.

questions.solution: 50% is half the circle: sector C, whose edges make a straight line through the centre. 25% is a quarter, a right angle: sector A. Of the two small sectors, the bigger one is 15% (banana): sector D. The smallest is 10% (papaya): sector B.

misconceptions.common: Mixing up the two smaller sectors. Find the half (50%) and the right angle (25%) first. Then 15% is the bigger of the two small sectors and 10% is the smallest.

questions.skill: reading pie charts and waffle charts

questions.prompt: The pie chart shows how 24 pupils voted for a class trip. Ahmad says: 'The Penang sector is 1/4 of the circle, so 4 pupils voted for Penang.' True or false: Ahmad is correct.

diagram.title: Class trip vote (24 pupils)
diagram.alt: Pie chart titled Class trip vote (24 pupils) with four sectors: Kuala Lumpur, Penang, Melaka and Langkawi. The Penang sector is marked as a right angle.

questions.solution: The Penang sector is a right angle, so it is 1/4 of the circle. Ahmad is right about that. But 1/4 of 24 = 24 ÷ 4 = 6, so 6 pupils voted for Penang, not 4. The statement is false. Trap: the 4 in 1/4 is not the number of pupils.

misconceptions.common: Mixing up the fraction with the number of pupils. 1/4 means 'divide the total by 4': 1/4 of 24 = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 pupils.

questions.skill: reading pie charts and waffle charts

questions.prompt: Mei Lin is drawing a pie chart of the favourite colours of 20 pupils. Each pupil gets the same angle. What angle does each pupil get?
questions.solution: A full circle is 360°. Share it equally among the 20 pupils: 360 ÷ 20 = 18°. Check: 20 x 18° = 360°.

misconceptions.0: You shared 100 among the 20 pupils, as if the pie chart were out of 100. A full circle is 360°, so share 360°: 360 ÷ 20 = 18°.
misconceptions.2: 20 is the number of pupils, not the angle. Share the 360° of the circle equally among the 20 pupils: 360 ÷ 20.
misconceptions.3: You subtracted 20 from 360. To share 360° equally among 20 pupils, divide: 360 ÷ 20 = 18°.

questions.prompt: Ahmad asked 40 customers at his stall to choose their favourite dessert. The table shows the results. He wants to draw a pie chart. What angle should the ais kacang sector be? Give your answer in degrees.
questions.solution: There are 40 customers and a full circle is 360°. Each customer gets 360 ÷ 40 = 9°. Ais kacang: 14 x 9° = 126°. Check all four: 126° + 108° + 72° + 54° = 360°.

misconceptions.common: Writing 14° (one degree per customer) or working out 360 ÷ 14. Divide 360 by the TOTAL number of customers (40) to get 9° each, then multiply by 14.

questions.prompt: The table shows the favourite colours of 24 pupils. Which pie chart shows this data correctly?
options: Pie chart A
Pie chart B
Pie chart C
Pie chart D
questions.solution: Each pupil gets 360 ÷ 24 = 15°. Blue: 12 x 15° = 180° (half the circle). Red: 6 x 15° = 90° (a right angle). Green: 4 x 15° = 60°. Yellow: 2 x 15° = 30°. Only pie chart D has blue as a half, red as the right angle, and green twice the size of yellow.

misconceptions.0: In this chart green is the right angle. Red is 6 out of 24 = 1/4, so red should be the right angle. Green (4 out of 24 = 1/6) should be smaller.
misconceptions.1: All four sectors are the same size here, but the colours were not chosen by the same number of pupils. Each sector must match its own number: blue, 12 out of 24, is half.
misconceptions.2: Here red is half the circle. Blue was chosen by 12 of the 24 pupils, so blue should be the half, and red (6 of 24) the quarter.

questions.prompt: The pie chart shows how 120 visitors travelled up Penang Hill one morning. How many visitors took the funicular train?

diagram.title: How 120 visitors went up Penang Hill
diagram.alt: Pie chart titled How 120 visitors went up Penang Hill: funicular train 144°, jeep 108°, walking 72°, car 36°.

questions.solution: A full circle is 360° for 120 visitors, so each visitor is 360 ÷ 120 = 3°. The funicular train sector is 144°, so 144 ÷ 3 = 48 visitors. (Or: 144/360 = 2/5, and 2/5 of 120 = 48.)

misconceptions.1: 3° is the angle for one visitor (360 ÷ 120 = 3). You stopped there. Now find how many lots of 3° are in 144°: 144 ÷ 3.
misconceptions.2: 72° is the angle of the walking sector, not the number of funicular visitors. Each visitor is 360 ÷ 120 = 3°, so the funicular's 144° stands for 144 ÷ 3 = 48 visitors.
misconceptions.3: 144 is the angle in degrees, not the number of visitors. Each visitor is 360 ÷ 120 = 3°, so 144° stands for 144 ÷ 3 visitors.

questions.skill: reading pie charts and waffle charts

questions.prompt: The pie chart shows the 80 durians sold at Stall P on Saturday. Stall Q sold 200 durians on Saturday. In Stall Q's pie chart, Musang King is 1/4, D24 is 1/2 and Red Prawn is 1/4. Select ALL the statements that are true.

diagram.title: Durians sold at Stall P (80 durians)
diagram.alt: Pie chart titled Durians sold at Stall P (80 durians): Musang King 1/2, D24 1/4, Red Prawn 1/4.

options: Stall P sold more Musang King durians than Stall Q, because its Musang King sector is bigger.
Stall Q sold more Musang King durians than Stall P.
Red Prawn is 1/4 of both pie charts, so both stalls sold the same number of Red Prawn durians.
Musang King is a bigger fraction of Stall P's sales than of Stall Q's sales.
Stall Q sold 80 more D24 durians than Stall P.
questions.solution: Work out the numbers from each stall's own total. Stall P (80): Musang King 1/2 of 80 = 40, D24 1/4 of 80 = 20, Red Prawn 20. Stall Q (200): Musang King 1/4 of 200 = 50, D24 1/2 of 200 = 100, Red Prawn 50. So Stall Q sold more Musang King (50 > 40) even though its sector is smaller; 1/2 is a bigger fraction than 1/4; and Stall Q sold 100 - 20 = 80 more D24. Trap: a bigger sector means a bigger fraction, not a bigger number.

misconceptions.0: A bigger sector means a bigger fraction of that stall's sales, not more durians. Stall P: 1/2 of 80 = 40. Stall Q: 1/4 of 200 = 50.
misconceptions.2: The same fraction of different totals gives different numbers. Stall P: 1/4 of 80 = 20. Stall Q: 1/4 of 200 = 50.
misconceptions.common: Comparing the sizes of the sectors. Work out the actual number of durians from each stall's own total before you compare.

questions.skill: reading pie charts and waffle charts

questions.prompt: The pie chart shows how some pupils travel to school. 15 pupils walk. Daniel says: 'So 90 pupils were asked altogether.' Is Daniel correct? Tick one answer with its reason.

diagram.title: How pupils travel to school
diagram.alt: Pie chart titled How pupils travel to school: walk 60°, bus 120°, car 144°, bicycle 36°.

options: No. 360 ÷ 15 = 24, so 24 pupils were asked.
No. 60 + 15 = 75, so 75 pupils were asked.
Yes. 60° is 1/6 of 360°, so the 15 walkers are 1/6 of the pupils, and 6 x 15 = 90.
Yes. 360 ÷ 4 sectors = 90.
questions.solution: The walk sector is 60°. 60/360 = 1/6, so the 15 walkers are 1/6 of all the pupils. The total is 6 x 15 = 90 pupils, so Daniel is correct. Check with another sector: each pupil is 360 ÷ 90 = 4°, and the bus sector 120° ÷ 4 = 30 pupils, a whole number. Trap: one option has the right total with a wrong reason.

misconceptions.0: You divided 360 by the number of walkers. That gives the angle per pupil only if 15 were the total. Use the fraction: 60° is 1/6 of 360°, so 15 is 1/6 of the total.
misconceptions.1: 60 is an angle in degrees and 15 is a number of pupils. They measure different things, so they must not be added.
misconceptions.3: 90 is the right total, but this reason is wrong. Dividing by the number of sectors only works when every sector is the same size, and these are not. Use the walking sector: 60° is 1/6 of 360°.

questions.skill: reading pie charts and waffle charts

questions.prompt: The pie chart shows how 80 customers paid at a pasar malam stall. How many more customers paid with cash than by card?

diagram.title: How 80 customers paid
diagram.alt: Pie chart titled How 80 customers paid: cash 40%, e-wallet 35%, card 15%, bank transfer 10%.

questions.solution: Cash: 40% of 80 = 80 ÷ 10 × 4 = 32 customers. Card: 10% of 80 is 8 and 5% is 4, so 15% of 80 = 8 + 4 = 12 customers. Difference: 32 - 12 = 20. (Or: 40% - 15% = 25%, and 25% of 80 = 20.) Trap: 25 is the difference in percent, not in customers.

misconceptions.common: Giving 25 (the difference in percentages) or 32 (the cash customers only). Find 40% of 80 and 15% of 80, then subtract; or find 25% of 80.

questions.skill: reading pie charts and waffle charts

questions.prompt: Wei Ming asked 20 pupils how many times they ate at a hawker centre last week. These are their answers: 2, 0, 3, 1, 2, 4, 2, 1, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 0, 2, 4, 1, 3, 2. He started the frequency table shown. What number should go in the box for 2 times?

diagram.title: Visits to a hawker centre last week

questions.solution: Go through the list and count every 2, crossing each one off: there are 7. Check: the frequencies must add up to 20 pupils: 3 + 4 + 7 + 4 + 2 = 20. (You can also find it as 20 - 3 - 4 - 4 - 2 = 7.)

misconceptions.common: Losing your place when counting. Cross off each answer as you count it, then check that all the frequencies add up to 20.

questions.skill: reading tally charts and frequency tables

questions.prompt: Match each set of data to the best way to show it. One way is not used.

left: The mass of a puppy, weighed on the first day of each month for a year
What fraction of the 200 durians sold at a stall were each of 4 varieties
Each pupil's leg length and how far that pupil can jump
Which pupils play football, which play badminton, which play both and which play neither

questions.solution: The puppy's mass is continuous data that changes over time: line graph. Fractions of the 200 durians are parts of one whole: pie chart. Leg length and jump distance are two measurements for each pupil, to look for a link: scatter graph. Football, badminton, both or neither are overlapping groups: Venn diagram. A tally chart is for recording counts while you collect data, not for showing a pattern, so it is not used.

misconceptions.common: Choosing a chart by the type of data alone. Ask what the data is about: change over time (line graph), parts of a whole (pie chart), a link between two measurements (scatter graph), or overlapping groups (Venn diagram).

questions.prompt: There are 40 pupils in Year 6. 22 play football, 15 play badminton and 8 play both. The Carroll diagram shows the 8 pupils who play both. How many pupils play neither football nor badminton?
questions.solution: Fill in the Carroll diagram. Plays football but not badminton: 22 - 8 = 14. Plays badminton but not football: 15 - 8 = 7. Pupils who play at least one sport: 8 + 14 + 7 = 29. Neither: 40 - 29 = 11. Check the football row: 8 + 14 = 22.

misconceptions.common: Working out 40 - 22 - 15 = 3. That takes the 8 pupils who play both away twice. Find football only (22 - 8 = 14) and badminton only (15 - 8 = 7) first, or answer 40 - 29 = 11.

questions.prompt: Kumar counted the cars that stopped at a petrol station between 7 am and 8 am each day. His results were: Monday 12, Tuesday 18, Wednesday 9, Thursday 15, Friday 6. He drew the bar chart shown, but he made one mistake. Which day's bar is wrong?

diagram.title: Cars at the petrol station, 7 am to 8 am
diagram.alt: A bar chart of the cars at the petrol station, with one bar for each day from Monday to Friday, on a scale from 0 to 20 going up in 2s.

options: Monday
Tuesday
Wednesday
Thursday
Friday
questions.solution: The scale goes up in 2s. Check each bar against the results. Monday 12, Tuesday 18 and Friday 6 end on their gridlines. Wednesday ends halfway between 8 and 10, which is 9: correct. Thursday ends on the line for 16, but the results say 15, so it should stop halfway between 14 and 16. Thursday's bar is wrong. Trap: a bar between two gridlines can be right, and a bar on a gridline can be wrong.

misconceptions.0: The Monday bar reaches the line for 12, which matches the table.
misconceptions.1: The Tuesday bar reaches the line for 18, which matches the table.
misconceptions.2: The Wednesday bar stops halfway between 8 and 10. Halfway is 9, which matches the table. A bar does not have to end on a gridline.
misconceptions.4: The Friday bar reaches the line for 6, which matches the table.

questions.skill: checking a chart against the data

questions.prompt: Rahim recorded how many durians each of 15 customers bought: 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 2, 1, 5, 3, 2, 4, 1, 3, 2. He drew the dot plot shown, but he left out one customer. How many durians did that customer buy?

diagram.title: Durians bought by each customer
diagram.alt: A dot plot of the number of durians bought by each customer, on a scale from 0 to 6. Each dot is one customer.

questions.solution: Tally the list: 1 durian: 3 customers; 2 durians: 5; 3 durians: 4; 4 durians: 2; 5 durians: 1 (15 in all). Count the dots: 1: 3; 2: 5; 3: 3; 4: 2; 5: 1 (14 in all). Only the column for 3 has one dot too few, so the missing customer bought 3 durians.

misconceptions.common: Looking at the tallest column, or counting dots without matching them to the list. Tally the list for each number, then compare each count with its column of dots: only one count is different.

questions.skill: checking a chart against the data

questions.prompt: Siti measured the heights of some sunflower plants. The frequency diagram shows her results. The modal class is the group with the most plants. Which group is the modal class?
options: 0 to under 20 cm
20 to under 40 cm
40 to under 60 cm
60 to under 80 cm
questions.solution: Find the tallest bar. It is the bar for 20 to under 40 cm, with 11 plants. The tallest bar shows the group with the most plants. So the modal class is 20 to under 40 cm.

misconceptions.0: This group has only 4 plants. Look for the TALLEST bar: that group has the most plants.
misconceptions.2: This bar (7 plants) is not the tallest. The bar for 20 to under 40 cm reaches 11.
misconceptions.3: This group has the tallest PLANTS, but only 3 of them. The modal class is the group with the most plants, so look for the tallest bar, not the biggest heights.

questions.prompt: Kumar asked some pupils how many minutes they spent on homework last night, to the nearest minute. He started the tally chart shown. One more pupil says 45 minutes. In which row should Kumar make the tally mark?
options: 0 to 14
questions.solution: 45 minutes is a whole number of minutes. Check each row: 45 is not between 30 and 44, because 44 is the last number in that row. 45 is the first number in the row 45 to 59. So the tally goes in 45 to 59.

misconceptions.0: 0 to 14 is for times from 0 to 14 minutes only. 45 is much bigger. Look for the row whose first and last numbers have 45 between them (or equal to one of them).
misconceptions.1: 15 to 29 stops at 29, so 45 does not fit. Find the row that starts with 45.
misconceptions.2: 30 to 44 stops at 44, so 45 is just past it. The row 45 to 59 starts at 45, so 45 goes there. Always check the first and last number of each group.

questions.prompt: Wei Ming timed 20 pupils solving a puzzle, to the nearest second. Here are the times in seconds: 21, 34, 27, 25, 38, 29, 22, 31, 25, 36, 30, 24, 28, 33, 29, 20, 35, 26, 32, 39. He is making the grouped frequency table shown. What number goes in the box for 25 to 29 seconds?
questions.solution: Go through the list in order and pick out every time from 25 to 29, including 25 and 29 themselves. They are 27, 25, 29, 25, 28, 29 and 26. That is 7 times. Check: the other groups have 4, 5 and 4, and 4 + 7 + 5 + 4 = 20, so every time has been counted once. The answer is 7.

misconceptions.common: The usual slip is with the boundary values: 25 and 29 both belong in 25 to 29 (there are two 25s and two 29s). Cross off each time as you count it, then check that all the groups add up to 20.

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows the number of visitors to a durian farm in Penang on five days. How many visitors were there on Wednesday?

diagram.title: Visitors to a durian farm
diagram.alt: A bar chart of the number of visitors to a durian farm from Monday to Friday. The scale goes from 0 to 100, labelled every 20, with small gridlines between the labels.

questions.solution: First work out what one small step is worth. From 60 to 80 is 20, and there are 4 small steps, so each step is 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Wednesday's bar ends 3 small steps above 60. 60 + 3 × 5 = 75 visitors.

misconceptions.common: It looks like each small step was counted as 1 (giving 63). Always work out the size of a small step first: 20 ÷ 4 gaps = 5. Then count up from the labelled line below the bar: 60, 65, 70, 75.

questions.prompt: The line graph shows the number of cars in a shopping-centre car park in KL one morning. How many cars were in the car park at 11 am?

diagram.title: Cars in the car park
diagram.alt: A line graph of the number of cars in a car park from 9 am to 1 pm. The scale goes from 0 to 300, labelled every 50, with small gridlines between the labels.

questions.solution: From 200 to 250 is 50, and there are 5 small steps, so each step is 50 ÷ 5 = 10. The point for 11 am is 3 small steps above 200. 200 + 3 × 10 = 230 cars.

misconceptions.0: 240 is the gridline just above the point. Count the small steps carefully from 200: 210, 220, 230.
misconceptions.2: It looks like each small step was taken as 5. There are 5 small steps between 200 and 250, so each one is 50 ÷ 5 = 10.
misconceptions.3: It looks like each small step was counted as 1. Each small step here is 50 ÷ 5 = 10, so 3 steps above 200 is 230.

questions.prompt: The frequency diagram shows how long the pupils in a swimming club took to swim one length. How many pupils took less than 30 seconds?

diagram.title: Time to swim one length
diagram.alt: A frequency diagram of the times pupils took to swim one length, in five groups from 20 to under 25 seconds up to 40 to under 45 seconds. The scale goes from 0 to 12, labelled every 2.

questions.solution: Less than 30 seconds means the groups 20 to under 25 and 25 to under 30. Read those bars: 3 and 8. Add them: 3 + 8 = 11 pupils. (The group 30 to under 35 starts at 30, so it is not less than 30.)

misconceptions.common: Two slips are common here: reading only the bar for 25 to under 30 (8), or adding the bar for 30 to under 35 as well. 'Less than 30 seconds' means every group that ends before 30, so add the first two bars.

questions.prompt: The table shows the number of satay sticks four stalls sold in an hour. Daniel will draw a bar chart. The vertical axis on his paper has 10 equal large squares. Which scale should he use, so that every bar fits and the tallest bar uses most of the height?

diagram.title: Satay sticks sold in an hour

options: 0 to 100, going up in 10s
0 to 10, going up in 1s
0 to 50, going up in 5s
0 to 500, going up in 50s
questions.solution: The largest number is 87, so the scale must go up to at least 87. 0 to 10 and 0 to 50 are too short. 0 to 100 and 0 to 500 both fit. On 0 to 500 the tallest bar would be less than 2 squares high, so the bars would be tiny and hard to compare. 0 to 100 in 10s is the best scale.

misconceptions.1: This scale stops at 10, but Stall B sold 87. Check the largest value first: the scale must reach it.
misconceptions.2: This scale stops at 50, so the bars for 64, 72 and 87 would not fit. The scale must reach at least 87.
misconceptions.3: Every bar fits, but 87 out of 500 is less than 2 of the 10 squares, so all the bars would be very short. Choose the smallest easy scale that still reaches the largest value.

questions.prompt: Daniel is drawing a bar chart. He writes these numbers up the vertical axis, with equal gaps between them: 0, 5, 10, 15, 25, 30, 35. True or false: Daniel's scale is correct.
questions.solution: On a scale, equal gaps must stand for equal amounts. Find the jump between each pair of numbers: 5, 5, 5, then 10 (from 15 to 25), then 5, 5. Daniel has left out 20, so one gap stands for 10 instead of 5. The statement is false: his scale is wrong.

misconceptions.common: The numbers do go up, but that is not enough. Check every jump: 15 to 25 is a jump of 10, while the others are 5. Daniel missed out 20, so bars above 15 would be drawn at the wrong height.

questions.prompt: The heights of 20 pupils in Year 6, to the nearest centimetre, are: 136, 141, 130, 145, 139, 140, 137, 148, 134, 143, 135, 149, 139, 140, 132, 146, 138, 144, 136, 142. Aisha groups them in a frequency table. Match each group to its frequency.
questions.solution: Sort the heights into the groups, ticking each one off. 130 to 134: 130, 134, 132 (3). 135 to 139: 136, 139, 137, 135, 139, 138, 136 (7). 140 to 144: 141, 140, 143, 140, 144, 142 (6). 145 to 149: 145, 148, 149, 146 (4). Check: 3 + 7 + 6 + 4 = 20. Watch the boundary values: 134 goes in 130 to 134, and 135 and 140 start new groups.

misconceptions.common: Check the heights on the edges of the groups: 134 and 139 are the LAST numbers in their groups, and 135, 140 and 145 are the FIRST numbers in theirs. If your frequencies do not add up to 20, a height has been missed or counted twice.

questions.prompt: The frequency diagram shows the marks the pupils in Year 6 scored in a quiz. Omar says, 'The modal class is 41 to 50, because those are the highest marks.' Is Omar correct? Tick one.
options: Yes. 41 to 50 is the modal class, because those are the highest marks.
No. The modal class is 13, because that is the height of the tallest bar.
No. The modal class is 31 to 40, because that group has the most pupils.
No. Grouped data cannot have a modal class.
questions.solution: The modal class is the group with the highest frequency (the most pupils). The tallest bar is 31 to 40, with 13 pupils. 41 to 50 has only 6 pupils. So Omar is not correct: the modal class is 31 to 40.

misconceptions.0: The modal class is not the group with the biggest marks. It is the group with the MOST pupils, so look for the tallest bar. 41 to 50 has only 6 pupils.
misconceptions.1: 13 is how many pupils are in the modal class, not the class itself. The modal class is the group under the tallest bar: 31 to 40.
misconceptions.3: Grouped data does have a modal class: the group with the highest frequency. Here it is 31 to 40.

questions.prompt: The frequency diagram shows how many minutes some pupils spent on their phones one evening. Rahim says, 'The diagram shows that exactly 3 pupils spent 100 minutes or more on their phones.' Is Rahim correct? Tick one.

diagram.title: Time spent on phones one evening
