options: No. The last bar shows 3 pupils spent from 90 to under 120 minutes, but not their exact times, so we cannot tell how many spent 100 minutes or more.
Yes. 100 is in the group 90 to under 120, so all 3 pupils in that group spent 100 minutes or more.
No. 10 pupils spent 100 minutes or more, because you add the last two bars: 7 + 3.
Yes. The last bar shows 3 pupils, so exactly 3 pupils spent 100 minutes or more.
questions.solution: The last bar shows 3 pupils in the group 90 to under 120 minutes. A pupil in that group could have spent 95 minutes or 115 minutes: the diagram does not show exact times. So somewhere from 0 to 3 pupils spent 100 minutes or more, and we cannot say exactly. Rahim is not correct.

misconceptions.1: Being in the group 90 to under 120 does not mean at least 100 minutes. A pupil in that group could have spent 92 minutes. Grouped data hides the exact values.
misconceptions.2: The bar for 60 to under 90 is all times under 90 minutes, so none of those 7 pupils spent 100 minutes or more. Only the last group could include 100 minutes or more.
misconceptions.3: The last bar is for 90 to under 120 minutes, not 100 minutes or more. Some of those 3 pupils may have spent less than 100 minutes, so we cannot say 'exactly 3'.

questions.prompt: The line graph shows the rainfall in a town in Malaysia each month for six months. How much more rain fell in March than in January? Give your answer in mm.

diagram.title: Monthly rainfall
diagram.alt: A line graph of the monthly rainfall in a town from January to June. The scale goes from 40 to 90 mm, labelled every 10, with small gridlines between the labels.

questions.solution: Each labelled step is 10 mm and there are 5 small steps, so each small step is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 mm. January is 3 small steps above 40: 40 + 6 = 46 mm. March is 2 small steps above 70: 70 + 4 = 74 mm. Difference: 74 - 46 = 28 mm.

misconceptions.common: If you got 29, you probably counted each small step as 1 mm (43 mm and 72 mm). Each small step here is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 mm. Read each value carefully, then subtract the smaller from the larger.

questions.prompt: Ahmad drew this line graph of the number of durians his stall sold each week. Look at where the vertical scale starts. Ahmad says, 'Sales in Week 4 were more than double the sales in Week 1.' Is Ahmad correct? Tick one.

diagram.title: Durians sold each week
diagram.alt: A line graph of the number of durians sold in Weeks 1 to 4. The vertical scale goes from 90 to 100, labelled every 2, with small gridlines every 1.

options: Yes. The point for Week 4 is about five times as high as the point for Week 1.
Yes. Sales went up every week.
No. Sales went down from Week 1 to Week 4.
No. Sales went from 92 to 100, only 8 more. The scale starts at 90, not 0, so the rise looks bigger than it is.
questions.solution: Read the values: Week 1 is 92 durians and Week 4 is 100 durians. Double 92 is 184, and 100 is far less than that. The rise is only 8 durians. The graph looks dramatic because the scale starts at 90 instead of 0. Ahmad is not correct.

misconceptions.0: The height above the bottom of the graph is misleading here, because the scale starts at 90, not 0. Read the actual numbers: 92 and 100. Double 92 is 184, so 100 is not double.
misconceptions.1: Sales did go up every week, but going up is not the same as doubling. 92 doubled is 184, and Week 4 was only 100.
misconceptions.2: The line goes up from left to right, so sales went up, from 92 to 100. The question is whether they doubled, and they did not.

questions.prompt: The table shows the number of visitors to four stalls at a school fun fair. Priya will draw a bar chart. Her vertical axis starts at 0 and has 10 equal steps. Select ALL the step sizes that would let every bar fit on her chart (even if some bars would be short).
options: Steps of 10
Steps of 15
Steps of 20
Steps of 25
Steps of 50
questions.solution: The largest value is 172, so the top of the scale must be at least 172. Top of each scale = 10 × step: steps of 10 reach 100, 15 reach 150, 20 reach 200, 25 reach 250, 50 reach 500. Only 200, 250 and 500 are 172 or more. So steps of 20, 25 and 50 all fit (steps of 20 uses the height best).

misconceptions.0: Steps of 10 only reach 10 × 10 = 100, but the cake stall had 172 visitors.
misconceptions.1: Steps of 15 reach 10 × 15 = 150. That fits the lucky dip (150) but not the cake stall (172). Always check the LARGEST value.
misconceptions.common: Work out the top of each scale (10 × the step) and compare it with the largest value, 172. Select every scale whose top is 172 or more.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the sets of five numbers that have a mode of 4, a median of 5 and a range of 6.
questions.solution: Put each set in order first, then check all three. 4, 4, 5, 7, 10: mode 4, median 5, range 10 - 4 = 6. 4, 4, 5, 8, 10 and 4, 4, 5, 9, 10 also work. 3, 4, 4, 5, 9 has median 4. 4, 4, 5, 5, 10 has two modes (4 and 5). 4, 4, 5, 9, 11 has range 7. So the answers are 10, 4, 7, 5, 4 and 4, 8, 5, 10, 4 and 9, 4, 4, 10, 5.

misconceptions.1: In this set the middle number as written is 5, but in order it is 3, 4, 4, 5, 9, so the median is 4. Always put the numbers in order before finding the median.
misconceptions.2: 4 and 5 both appear twice, so this set has two modes, 4 and 5. The mode must be 4 only.
misconceptions.4: The mode and median are right, but the range is 11 - 4 = 7, not 6.
misconceptions.common: Sort each set into order first. Then check all three facts: the most common number, the middle number, and largest minus smallest. A set must pass all three. Two of the correct sets do not look right until they are sorted.

questions.prompt: The dot plot shows how many times each pupil in a group went swimming last month. Each dot is one pupil. Work out the mean number of times a pupil went swimming.

diagram.title: Swimming trips last month
diagram.alt: A dot plot of how many times each pupil went swimming last month, on a scale from 0 to 6. Each dot is one pupil.

questions.solution: Count the dots: 3 + 5 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 15 pupils. Find the total number of swims: 0 × 3 + 1 × 5 + 2 × 2 + 3 × 2 + 4 × 1 + 5 × 1 + 6 × 1 = 0 + 5 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 30. Mean = total ÷ number of pupils = 30 ÷ 15 = 2.

misconceptions.common: Common slips: stopping at the total (30), dividing by 7 (the number of marks on the scale) instead of 15 (the number of pupils), giving the mode or median (1), or taking the middle of the scale (3). Mean = total of all the values ÷ how many values there are, and each dot is one value.

questions.prompt: The table shows the times, in seconds, that Aisha and Rahim took in five 100 m races. Wei Ming says, 'Rahim is usually faster, but Aisha is more consistent.' Use the median and the range to decide. Is Wei Ming correct? Tick one.
options: No. Aisha is usually faster, because her median time (18 s) is higher.
No. Rahim is more consistent, because his range (5 s) is bigger.
Yes. Rahim's median time (16 s) is lower, so he is usually faster, and Aisha's range (2 s) is smaller, so her times are more consistent.
Yes. Rahim's range (5 s) is bigger, so he is usually faster, and Aisha's median (18 s) is higher, so she is more consistent.
questions.solution: Put the times in order. Aisha: 17, 17, 18, 18, 19, so median 18 s and range 19 - 17 = 2 s. Rahim: 15, 16, 16, 18, 20, so median 16 s and range 20 - 15 = 5 s. In a race a lower time is faster, so Rahim is usually faster. A smaller range means the times are closer together, so Aisha is more consistent. Wei Ming is correct.

misconceptions.0: In a race, a LOWER time is faster. Aisha's median time (18 s) is higher than Rahim's (16 s), so she is usually slower.
misconceptions.1: A bigger range means the times are MORE spread out, so Rahim is less consistent. The smaller range (Aisha's 2 s) shows the more consistent runner.
misconceptions.3: The two measures are swapped. The median (an average) tells you who is usually faster; the range tells you who is more consistent. Wei Ming is right, but for the reasons in the other 'Yes' option.

questions.skill: comparing with an average and the range

questions.prompt: The scatter graph shows how many hours some pupils revised and their score in a test out of 50. One pupil revised for 6 hours. What was this pupil's test score?

diagram.title: Revision time and test score
diagram.alt: A scatter graph of hours of revision and test score for 8 pupils.

questions.solution: Find 6 on the bottom axis (hours of revision). Go straight up to the cross above 6. Go across to the side axis and read the score. Each gridline on the side is 5 marks, and the cross is on the line for 35. The pupil scored 35.

misconceptions.common: Check that you are reading the cross directly above 6, not a neighbour, and count the side gridlines in 5s. Reading the line next to it gives 30 or 40.

questions.prompt: The scatter graph shows the age and the price of some second-hand cars at a car dealer in Kuala Lumpur. Which sentence describes the relationship shown?

diagram.title: Age and price of used cars
diagram.alt: A scatter graph of the age and price of 9 used cars.

options: As the age of the car goes up, the price goes up.
As the age of the car goes up, the price goes down.
There is no relationship between the age and the price.
All the cars cost about the same.
questions.solution: Look at the crosses from left to right. On the left (newer cars) the crosses are high; on the right (older cars) they are low. So the points go down from left to right: as the age goes up, the price goes down.

misconceptions.0: The crosses start high on the left and end low on the right, so they go DOWN. When the points go up from left to right, both values go up together.
misconceptions.2: No relationship would look like crosses scattered everywhere. Here they follow a clear line going down.
misconceptions.3: Read the side axis: the prices go from about RM 80 thousand down to about RM 20 thousand. That is a big difference.

questions.prompt: The scatter graph shows the shoe size and the spelling test score (out of 20) of 12 pupils. True or false: the graph shows that pupils with bigger feet scored higher in the spelling test.

diagram.title: Shoe size and spelling score
diagram.alt: A scatter graph of shoe size and spelling score for 12 pupils.

questions.solution: Look at each shoe size. Pupils with size 3 scored 8 and 15; pupils with size 8 scored 9 and 17. For every shoe size there are high and low scores. The crosses are scattered with no pattern going up or down, so there is no relationship. The statement is false.

misconceptions.common: One high score on the right (size 8, 17 marks) does not make a pattern. Look at ALL the crosses: they are scattered, so shoe size and spelling score are not related.

questions.prompt: Kumar is drawing a scatter graph of the mass and the price of watermelons at a pasar malam. He has plotted 6 watermelons, as shown. His next watermelon has a mass of 4 kg and costs RM 14. How should he plot it?
options: Go across to 4 kg, then up to RM 12.
Go across to 14, then up to 4.
Go across to 4 kg, then up to RM 14.
Go across to 5 kg, then up to RM 14.
questions.solution: Mass is on the bottom axis, so go across to 4 kg first. Price is on the side axis, so then go up to RM 14. Each side gridline is RM 2, so RM 14 is the 7th line up. Mark a cross where 4 kg and RM 14 meet.

misconceptions.0: Each gridline on the price axis is RM 2. RM 12 is one line too low: count up to RM 14.
misconceptions.1: You swapped the two values. The bottom axis is mass, so go across to 4 kg; the side axis is price, so go up to RM 14.
misconceptions.3: The mass is 4 kg, not 5 kg. Check the number on the bottom axis before you go up.

questions.prompt: The scatter graph shows how many hours 10 pupils spend reading each week and how many books they read in a term. How many of these pupils read more than 10 books?

diagram.title: Reading time and books read
diagram.alt: A scatter graph of reading time and books read for 10 pupils.

questions.solution: Find 10 on the side axis (books read) and imagine a line across the graph there. Count the crosses ABOVE that line: they are at 12, 14, 12, 16 and 18 books. That is 5 pupils.

misconceptions.common: Books read is on the side axis. Count the crosses above the 10-books line, not the ones near 10 hours on the bottom axis.

questions.prompt: Mei Lin measured six friends. Siti: 135 cm, 32 kg. Arjun: 140 cm, 34 kg. Priya: 145 cm, 38 kg. Omar: 150 cm, 40 kg. Lina: 155 cm, 44 kg. Ahmad: 160 cm, 46 kg. She plotted the scatter graph shown, but one point is in the wrong place. Whose point is wrong?
options: Arjun
Omar
Ahmad
Lina
questions.solution: Check each friend's height on the bottom axis and mass on the side axis. There is no cross above 155 cm, but there are two crosses above 150 cm: one at 40 kg (Omar, correct) and one at 44 kg. Lina's mass is 44 kg, so that cross is hers, plotted at 150 cm instead of 155 cm. Lina's point is wrong.

misconceptions.0: Arjun's cross is at 140 cm and 34 kg, which matches his data. Check every friend: there is no cross above 155 cm, so look for Lina's.
misconceptions.1: There are two crosses above 150 cm. Omar's is the one at 40 kg, which is correct. The other one, at 44 kg, belongs to Lina and should be above 155 cm.
misconceptions.2: Ahmad's cross is at 160 cm and 46 kg, which matches his data. Each side gridline is 2 kg, so count carefully.

questions.prompt: The scatter graph shows how many hours 8 pupils practise badminton each week and how many matches each won this year. Siti: 1 h, 2 wins. Wei Ming: 2 h, 3 wins. Aisha: 3 h, 5 wins. Daniel: 4 h, 6 wins. Priya: 5 h, 8 wins. Kumar: 6 h, 9 wins. Rahim: 7 h, 11 wins. Mei Lin: 8 h, 2 wins. One point does not fit the pattern of the others. Write the name of the pupil whose point it is.
questions.solution: Most crosses go up from left to right: more practice goes with more wins. One cross is far below this pattern, at 8 hours and 2 wins. In the list, the pupil who practises 8 hours and won 2 matches is Mei Lin. (Siti also won 2, but she practises only 1 hour, so her cross fits the pattern.)

misconceptions.common: The odd point is not just the lowest one: Siti also won 2 matches but practises only 1 hour, so she fits the pattern. Look for the cross that is far from the line the other crosses make: 8 hours and only 2 wins.

questions.prompt: Arjun cycles in Penang. The scatter graph shows the distance and the time of 8 of his rides. Use the pattern to choose the best estimate of the time for a 7 km ride.
options: About 35 minutes
About 15 minutes
About 50 minutes
About 7 minutes
questions.solution: There is no cross at 7 km, so use the pattern. The 6 km ride took about 29 minutes and the 8 km ride about 41 minutes. A 7 km ride should take somewhere in between, so about 35 minutes is the best estimate.

misconceptions.1: 15 minutes is about the time for a 3 km ride. Find 7 km on the bottom axis and look at the crosses on each side of it.
misconceptions.2: Even the 9 km ride took less than 45 minutes, so a shorter 7 km ride should take less time than that.
misconceptions.3: 7 is the distance, not the time. Use the crosses near 7 km to read the time on the side axis.

questions.prompt: Wei Ming recorded the number of pages in 5 books and the number of days he took to read each one. He drew the scatter graph shown from one of the tables below. Which table did he use?
options: Table A
Table B
Table C
Table D
questions.solution: Read each cross: across for pages, up for days. The crosses are at 100 pages, 2 days; 150, 4; 200, 5; 250, 6; 300, 8. Now check every row of every table. Table A has 200 pages taking 6 days, Table B has 175 pages, and Table D has 200 pages taking 6 days and 250 pages taking 5 days. Only Table C matches all five crosses.

misconceptions.0: Table A says the 200-page book took 6 days, but the cross above 200 is at 5 days. Check every row, not just the first few.
misconceptions.1: Table B has a book with 175 pages, but there is no cross between the 150 and 200 gridlines. The cross is on the 150 line.
misconceptions.3: Table D swaps the days for the 200-page and 250-page books. The cross above 200 is at 5 days and the cross above 250 is at 6 days.

questions.prompt: The scatter graph shows the marks of 12 pupils in Test 1 and Test 2. Both tests were out of 50. How many pupils scored at least 30 marks in Test 2?

diagram.title: Test 1 and Test 2 marks
diagram.alt: A scatter graph of Test 1 and Test 2 marks for 12 pupils.

questions.solution: Test 2 is on the side axis. 'At least 30' means 30 or more, so the crosses ON the 30 line count too. There are 3 crosses on the 30 line, and 4 crosses above it (at 35, 35, 40 and 45). 3 + 4 = 7 pupils.

misconceptions.common: If you got 4, you counted only the crosses above 30. 'At least 30' includes pupils who scored exactly 30, so the 3 crosses on the 30 line count as well. Also check you used the Test 2 axis (up the side).

questions.prompt: A swimming coach recorded the number of training sessions in a month and the number of lengths each swimmer could swim without stopping. The scatter graph shows 6 swimmers. Three more swimmers are: Lina, 6 sessions, 10 lengths. Ahmad, 12 sessions, 14 lengths. Priya, 18 sessions, 16 lengths. Which graph shows all 9 swimmers plotted correctly?
options: Graph A
Graph B
Graph C
Graph D
questions.solution: Plot each new swimmer: across for sessions, up for lengths (each gridline is 2). Lina goes at (6, 10), Ahmad at (12, 14) and Priya at (18, 16). Graph A has Lina at 10 sessions and 6 lengths (swapped). Graph B is missing Priya, so it has only 8 crosses. Graph C has Ahmad at 16 lengths. Graph D has all three new crosses in the right places, so it is correct. Trap: check that ALL three points are there.

misconceptions.0: In Graph A, Lina's cross is at 10 sessions and 6 lengths. Her values are the other way round: across to 6 sessions, then up to 10 lengths.
misconceptions.1: Graph B has only 8 crosses: Priya (18 sessions, 16 lengths) is missing. When you plot several points, count them at the end.
misconceptions.2: In Graph C, Ahmad's cross is at 16 lengths, one gridline too high. He swam 14 lengths.

questions.prompt: The scatter graph shows the height and the hand span of 10 pupils. Aisha says, 'Taller pupils always have bigger hand spans.' Is Aisha correct? Choose the answer with the correct reason.
options: Yes. The points go up from left to right, so a taller pupil always has a bigger hand span.
No. There is no relationship between height and hand span.
No. Taller pupils usually have bigger hand spans, but not always: the pupil who is 146 cm tall has a smaller hand span (15 cm) than the pupil who is 142 cm tall (17 cm).
Yes. The tallest pupil has the biggest hand span.
questions.solution: The crosses go up from left to right, so taller pupils USUALLY have bigger hand spans. But 'always' means there are no exceptions. The pupil who is 146 cm tall has a hand span of 15 cm, while a shorter pupil, 142 cm, has 17 cm. One exception is enough, so Aisha is not correct. Trap: a pattern on a scatter graph tells you what usually happens, not what always happens.

misconceptions.0: The points do go up, but that shows what usually happens. Compare 142 cm (17 cm span) with 146 cm (15 cm span): the taller pupil has the smaller hand span, so 'always' is wrong.
misconceptions.1: There is a relationship: the crosses go up from left to right. Aisha is wrong only because of the word 'always'.
misconceptions.3: One pair of values does not prove 'always'. You need to check every pair. The 146 cm pupil has a smaller span than the 142 cm pupil.

questions.prompt: Which of these sets of data could be shown on a scatter graph? Select ALL the correct answers.
options: The height and the mass of each pupil in a class
The favourite fruit and the favourite colour of each pupil
The hours of rain and the number of umbrellas a shop sold, on each day in a month
The number of pupils in each class who walk to school
The colour and the age of each car in a car park
The age and the height of each tree in a park
questions.solution: A scatter graph needs TWO number values for each person or thing, so that each one becomes a point (across, up). Height and mass: two numbers for each pupil. Hours of rain and umbrellas sold: two numbers for each day. Age and height: two numbers for each tree. Fruit and colour are words, not numbers. 'Pupils in each class who walk' is only one number per class (a bar chart). Colour is not a number, so the cars cannot be plotted.

misconceptions.1: Favourite fruit and favourite colour are categories (words), not numbers, so they cannot be placed on number axes.
misconceptions.3: This is only ONE number for each class. A scatter graph needs two numbers for each item; this data suits a bar chart.
misconceptions.4: The age is a number, but the colour is not. Both values must be numbers to plot a point.
misconceptions.common: Check each answer: does every person or thing have TWO number values? If yes, it can be a scatter graph.

questions.prompt: The scatter graph shows the screen time and the sleep of 14 pupils on one school night. How many pupils had MORE than 2 hours of screen time AND slept LESS than 8 hours?

diagram.title: Screen time and sleep
diagram.alt: A scatter graph of screen time and sleep for 14 pupils.

questions.solution: Each gridline is half an hour. A pupil counts only if BOTH are true: screen time to the RIGHT of the 2 hour line (not on it) and sleep BELOW the 8 hour line (not on it). The crosses at 2 hours (7.5 h sleep), and at 8 hours of sleep (2.5 h and 4 h screen time) are on a line, so they do not count. The pupils who count are at (3, 7.5), (3.5, 7), (4.5, 7.5), (5, 6.5) and (5.5, 7). That is 5 pupils.

misconceptions.common: If you got 8, you counted the crosses that sit exactly on the 2 hour line or the 8 hour line. 'More than 2' does not include 2, and 'less than 8' does not include 8. Also check that each cross meets BOTH conditions, not just one.

questions.prompt: The scatter graph shows the maths and science test marks (out of 50) of 10 pupils. Select ALL the statements that are true.

diagram.title: Maths and science marks
diagram.alt: A scatter graph of maths and science marks for 10 pupils.

options: In general, pupils who did well in maths also did well in science.
The pupil with the lowest maths mark also had the lowest science mark.
Exactly two pupils got the same mark in maths as in science.
More pupils scored higher in science than in maths.
Every pupil who scored more than 35 in maths scored at least 40 in science.
questions.solution: 1: The crosses go up from left to right: true. 2: The lowest maths mark is 15, and that pupil scored 20 in science; the lowest science mark (15) belongs to the pupil with 20 in maths: false. 3: Same mark in both: (25, 25) and (40, 40), exactly two: true. 4: Science higher: (15, 20), (20, 25), (30, 35), (40, 45) = 4 pupils; maths higher: (20, 15), (30, 25), (35, 30), (45, 40) = 4 pupils. 4 is not more than 4: false. 5: More than 35 in maths: (40, 40), (40, 45), (45, 40), all at least 40: true. True: 1, 3 and 5.

misconceptions.1: The cross furthest left (15 in maths) is at 20 in science. The lowest cross (15 in science) is a different pupil, with 20 in maths. Check both axes.
misconceptions.3: Count both groups: 4 pupils scored higher in science and 4 scored higher in maths. The two pupils on (25, 25) and (40, 40) scored the same. 4 is not more than 4.
misconceptions.common: Check every statement against the graph one at a time, counting crosses carefully. Watch the words 'exactly', 'more than' and 'at least'.

questions.prompt: Daniel's athletics club recorded each runner's hours of training each week and their time to run 100 m in seconds. Daniel found that the more a runner trains, the faster they run. Which graph shows this?
options: Graph A
Graph B
Graph C
Graph D
questions.solution: Running faster means taking FEWER seconds to run 100 m. So as the hours of training go up, the time goes down. The crosses should go down from left to right. That is Graph B. Trap: 'faster' sounds like 'more', but a faster time is a smaller number of seconds.

misconceptions.0: In Graph A the times go UP, so runners who train more take more seconds, which means they are slower. Faster means fewer seconds.
misconceptions.2: Graph C has no pattern, so it would show that training makes no difference. Daniel found a clear link.
misconceptions.3: In Graph D every runner takes the same time, whatever their training. Daniel found that more training goes with faster times.

questions.prompt: The line graph shows the price of 1 kg of durians at a stall over six weeks of the durian season. Which sentence describes the trend?

diagram.title: Price of 1 kg of durians
diagram.alt: A line graph of the price of 1 kg of durians over six weeks.

options: The price went up every week.
The price stayed the same.
The price went up, then went down.
The price went down every week.
questions.solution: Follow the line from Week 1 to Week 6. Every part of the line slopes down: RM 60, 55, 50, 40, 35, 30. So the price went down every week.

misconceptions.0: Read the line from left to right (Week 1 to Week 6). It starts high and ends low, so the price went down.
misconceptions.1: A price that stays the same would be a flat line. This line slopes down.
misconceptions.2: Check each step of the line. It never goes up: it slopes down from Week 1 all the way to Week 6.

questions.prompt: Siti let a ball roll down the same ramp from the same height 5 times and timed it with a stopwatch. Her results are in the table. Why are the times not all the same?

diagram.title: Time for the ball to roll down the ramp

options: Small things change each time, such as exactly when she started and stopped the stopwatch.
The ramp was a different length each time.
Every result except one must be a mistake.
A stopwatch can only measure whole seconds.
questions.solution: The ramp and the height did not change. Small things change each time: exactly when Siti pressed start and stop, and exactly how she let go of the ball. This is why repeated measurements are slightly different. It is normal, and it is why scientists repeat measurements.

misconceptions.1: Siti used the same ramp and the same height every time. The differences come from small changes in how she timed it and let go.
misconceptions.2: The results are all close together (2.4 to 2.7 seconds). Small differences like this are normal when you measure something several times.
misconceptions.3: Her stopwatch measured tenths of a second (2.4, 2.6 ...). The differences come from small changes each try.

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows how many packets of nasi lemak two stalls sold from Monday to Friday. On how many days did Stall A sell more than Stall B?

diagram.title: Nasi lemak sold
diagram.alt: A bar chart comparing nasi lemak sold by Stall A and Stall B from Monday to Friday.

questions.solution: Compare the two bars for each day. Mon: A 40, B 35, A more. Tue: A 35, B 40, B more. Wed: A 50, B 45, A more. Thu: both 45, the same. Fri: A 30, B 35, B more. Stall A sold more on 2 days (Monday and Wednesday).

misconceptions.common: On Thursday both stalls sold 45, so Stall A did not sell MORE that day. Count only the days where A's bar is taller.

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows how many library books each year group borrowed in one month. True or false: Year 5 borrowed twice as many books as Year 3.

diagram.title: Library books borrowed
diagram.alt: A bar chart of library books borrowed by Years 3 to 6.

questions.solution: Read the bars: Year 3 borrowed 40 books and Year 5 borrowed 80 books. Twice 40 is 80. So the statement is true.

misconceptions.common: Read the Year 3 and Year 5 bars carefully (each small gridline is 5 books): 40 and 80. Then check: 40 x 2 = 80, so it is exactly twice.

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows the rainfall in Ipoh each day for one week. Lina works out that the mean is 15 mm. She concludes: 'On a typical day this week, it rained about 15 mm.' What is the best reason why her conclusion is not reliable?
options: Thursday's 80 mm is much more than the other days. This one unusual value makes the mean bigger than a typical day.
Her mean is wrong. It should be 80 mm.
She should have drawn a pie chart instead.
It did not rain on two days, so the mean cannot be worked out.
questions.solution: Read the bars: 5, 0, 10, 80, 5, 0 and 5 mm. The mean is (5 + 0 + 10 + 80 + 5 + 0 + 5) ÷ 7 = 105 ÷ 7 = 15 mm, so her mean is right. But one day, Thursday, had 80 mm, far more than any other day. That one unusual value pulls the mean up. On every other day it rained 10 mm or less, so 15 mm is not typical.

misconceptions.1: 80 mm is the largest value, not the mean. The mean is 105 ÷ 7 = 15 mm, so her calculation is right. The problem is that 15 mm is not typical.
misconceptions.2: Changing the chart does not change the data. The problem is the one very rainy day, which pulls the mean up.
misconceptions.3: Days with 0 mm still count: add 0 and divide by 7 as usual. The real problem is Thursday's 80 mm.

questions.prompt: Before his survey, Kumar predicted: 'More than half of my class will choose football as their favourite sport.' The table shows his results. Was his prediction correct? Choose the answer with the correct reason.
options: Yes, because football is the most popular sport.
Yes, because 14 out of 28 is half.
No, because 14 is exactly half of 28, not more than half.
No, because fewer pupils chose football than badminton and swimming together.
questions.solution: Total pupils: 14 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 28. Half of 28 is 14. Exactly 14 pupils chose football. 'More than half' would need 15 or more, so his prediction was not correct. Trap: football is the most popular, but 'most popular' is not the same as 'more than half'.

misconceptions.0: Football is the most popular, but the prediction was 'more than half'. 14 out of 28 is exactly half, so it is not more than half.
misconceptions.1: You worked out the half correctly, but exactly half is not MORE than half. More than half would be 15 or more pupils.
misconceptions.3: Badminton and swimming together are 8 + 4 = 12, which is less than 14. The real reason is that 14 is exactly half of 28.

questions.prompt: Omar grew two bean plants. Plant A was given plant food and Plant B was not. The line graph shows their heights each week. Select ALL the statements that are true.

diagram.title: Heights of two bean plants
diagram.alt: A line graph of the heights of Plant A and Plant B from Week 0 to Week 5.

options: Plant A was taller than Plant B every week.
The difference between the heights was greatest in Week 5.
Plant B grew the same amount every week.
Plant A grew 4 cm between Week 2 and Week 3.
Plant B was taller than Plant A in Week 1.
Plant A grew more between Week 4 and Week 5 than in any other week.
questions.solution: Read the heights. Plant A: 4, 6, 9, 13, 16, 20 cm. Plant B: 4, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13 cm. Week 0 they are equal and in Week 1 Plant B is taller, so A was not taller every week. Differences: 0, 1 (in Week 1 Plant B is 1 cm taller), 1, 3, 4, 7, greatest in Week 5 (true). Plant B grew 3, 1, 2, 2, 1 cm: not the same each week. Plant A from Week 2 to 3: 13 - 9 = 4 cm (true). Week 1: B 7 cm, A 6 cm (true). Plant A grew 2, 3, 4, 3, 4 cm: Week 4 to 5 (4 cm) ties with Week 2 to 3, so it is not MORE than every other week. True: statements 2, 4 and 5.

misconceptions.0: Check every week, including Week 0 and Week 1. In Week 0 the plants were the same height, and in Week 1 Plant B was taller.
misconceptions.2: Work out each week's growth for Plant B: 3, 1, 2, 2, 1 cm. These are not all the same.
misconceptions.5: Plant A grew 4 cm from Week 4 to 5, but it also grew 4 cm from Week 2 to 3. A tie is not 'more than any other week'.
misconceptions.common: Test each statement against the graph one by one, and watch the words 'every', 'greatest' and 'more than'.

questions.prompt: The bar chart shows how many pupils walk to school at two schools in Shah Alam. School A has 600 pupils and School B has 150 pupils. Mei Lin concludes: 'Walking to school is more popular at School A than at School B.' Is she correct? Choose the answer with the correct reason.
options: Yes, because 60 is more than 45.
No. 60 out of 600 is 1/10 of School A, but 45 out of 150 is 3/10 of School B, so walking is more popular at School B.
Yes, because School A is bigger, so more of its pupils walk.
No, because you can never compare two schools of different sizes.
questions.solution: Read the bars: 60 pupils walk at School A and 45 at School B. The schools are different sizes, so compare fractions. School A: 60 out of 600 = 1/10. School B: 45 out of 150 = 3/10. 3/10 is more than 1/10, so a bigger share of School B walks. Mei Lin is not correct. Trap: a bigger number is not a bigger share when the totals are different.

misconceptions.0: 60 is more than 45, but School A has 4 times as many pupils. Compare fractions: 60/600 = 1/10 and 45/150 = 3/10.
misconceptions.2: A bigger school will usually have more walkers just because it has more pupils. To compare fairly, find the fraction of each school who walk.
misconceptions.3: You can compare them fairly by using fractions or percentages of each school: 1/10 for School A and 3/10 for School B.

questions.prompt: Wei Ming dropped a ball from the same height 5 times and measured how high it bounced. The dot plot shows his results. Select ALL the statements that are true.

diagram.title: Bounce height of the ball
diagram.alt: A dot plot of 5 bounce heights.

options: Most of the results are slightly different because small things change each time, such as how he let go and how he read the ruler.
The 64 cm result is very different from the others, so he should check it by dropping the ball again.
The results are not all the same, so the experiment is useless.
The mean, 48 cm, is a good typical value, because it uses every result.
The median, 44 cm, describes a typical bounce better than the mean does.
The range of the results is 64 cm.
questions.solution: The results are 42, 44, 44, 46 and 64 cm. Small changes each time make repeated results differ a little (statement 1 true). 64 cm is far from the rest, so it should be checked (statement 2 true). Different results do not make an experiment useless. Mean = 240 ÷ 5 = 48 cm, which is bigger than 4 of the 5 results, because the 64 pulls it up, so it is not typical. Median = 44 cm, in the middle of the close results (statement 5 true). Range = 64 - 42 = 22 cm, not 64 cm. True: 1, 2 and 5.

misconceptions.2: Repeated measurements nearly always differ a little. Scientists repeat them and look at all the results; that makes the experiment better, not useless.
misconceptions.3: The mean does use every result, but the unusual 64 cm pulls it up to 48 cm, which is more than 4 of the 5 results. The median, 44 cm, is more typical here.
misconceptions.5: 64 cm is the largest value, not the range. Range = largest - smallest = 64 - 42 = 22 cm.
misconceptions.common: Check each statement: work out the mean, median and range from the dots, then decide which statements are true.

questions.prompt: The line graph shows the number of visitors to Penang Hill each day for one week. True or false: on Saturday there were more than twice as many visitors as the mean number of visitors per day from Monday to Friday.

diagram.title: Visitors to Penang Hill
diagram.alt: A line graph of visitors to Penang Hill from Monday to Sunday.

questions.solution: Read Monday to Friday (each small gridline is 50): 150, 200, 150, 250, 300. Total = 1050. Mean = 1050 ÷ 5 = 210 visitors. Twice the mean = 420. Saturday had 450 visitors, and 450 is more than 420. So the statement is true.

misconceptions.common: Find the mean of the FIVE weekdays first (1050 ÷ 5 = 210), then double it (420) and compare with Saturday (450). Do not include Saturday or Sunday in the mean, and read the half gridlines (50s) carefully.
